theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.etale_of_etale_height_one_of_regularLocalRing
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, group theory

a.states: Let R be a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal is generated by dim R elements, so that R is regular, with dim R ≥ 1 and R not a field. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite and faithful R-algebra. If A ⊗_R R_p is étale over R_p for every prime p of R of height one, then A is étale over R.
a.notation: R regular local, dim R ≥ 1, A normal domain finite and faithful over R, A_p étale over R_p for all primes p with ht p = 1 ⟹ A étale over R
a.known_as: the Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus
a.reference: M. Nagata, On the purity of branch loci in regular local rings, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 3 (1959)
a.vacuity: The hypothesis that R is not a field already follows from dim R ≥ 1, and when dim R = 1 the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal, while for dim R ≥ 2 none found.
a.why: A normal domain finite over R is the integral closure of R in its own fraction field, and étaleness at a height-one prime forces that field to be separable over the fraction field of R, so this is purity of the branch locus as Nagata states it.

b.states: Let R be a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal needs exactly dim R generators, which makes R a regular local ring, with dim R ≥ 1 and R not a field. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite and faithful R-algebra. If R_p ⊗_R A is étale over R_p for every prime p of R of height 1, then A is étale over R.
b.known_as: Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus for a finite normal domain over a regular local ring
b.vacuity: Nothing empties the statement, but in dimension one the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal up to the isomorphism of R with its localization there, and the assumption that R is not a field repeats dim R ≥ 1.

check.known_as: Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus
check.vacuity: None found, although in dimension one the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal up to the isomorphism of R with its localization there.
check.note: The assumption that R is not a field repeats the assumption dim R ≥ 1, and étaleness at the height-one primes already gives étaleness at the generic point, which purity needs.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.BranchPurity.finiteRing_sq_sub_mul_sq_eq_of_card
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, group theory

a.states: For every natural number n, let R be a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal needs exactly n generators and whose Krull dimension equals that number of generators, so that R is regular, and assume that R is not a field. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite and faithful R-algebra. If A ⊗_R R_p is étale over R_p for every prime p of R of height one, then A is étale over R. The name of the theorem refers to finite rings and to a difference of squares, which does not describe this content.
a.notation: R regular local and not a field, A normal domain finite and faithful over R, A_p étale over R_p for all primes p with ht p = 1 ⟹ A étale over R
a.known_as: the Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus
a.reference: M. Nagata, On the purity of branch loci in regular local rings, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 3 (1959)
a.vacuity: The variable n only names the number of generators and constrains nothing, and when dim R = 1 the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal, while for dim R ≥ 2 none found.
a.why: The statement is Theorem 56 without the hypothesis dim R ≥ 1, which costs nothing because a regular local ring that is not a field has positive dimension, so it is again purity of the branch locus.

b.states: For every natural number n, let R be a Noetherian local domain that is not a field and whose maximal ideal needs exactly n generators, with n equal to the Krull dimension of R. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite and faithful R-algebra. If R_p ⊗_R A is étale over R_p for every prime p of R of height 1, then A is étale over R. The name speaks of finite rings and squares, but the statement is the same purity claim as Theorem 56, with the embedding dimension named n.
b.known_as: Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus for a finite normal domain over a regular local ring
b.vacuity: Nothing empties the statement, but when R has dimension one the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal up to the isomorphism of R with its localization there.

check.known_as: Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus
check.vacuity: None found, although in dimension one the conclusion is the hypothesis at the maximal ideal up to the isomorphism of R with its localization there.
check.note: The variable n only names the number of generators of the maximal ideal and constrains nothing, the hypothesis dim R ≥ 1 of Theorem 56 is dropped because a regular local ring that is not a field has positive dimension, and the name of the theorem does not describe its content.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.OddGenus.orthonormal_of_diagonal
theorems.areas: number fields

a.states: Let K be a number field containing θ with θ² = −d for a positive integer d and such that every element of K is a + bθ with rational a and b, so that K is the imaginary quadratic field ℚ(√−d), and let σ be a ring endomorphism of K with σ(θ) = −θ, which is complex conjugation. Let h be a form on a K-vector space V that is K-linear in the first argument and σ-semilinear in the second. If vectors v_1,…,v_r satisfy h(v_i, v_j) = a_i δ_{ij} with positive rationals a_i whose product is a square in ℚ, then there are vectors e_1,…,e_r in V with h(e_i, e_j) = δ_{ij}.
a.notation: K = ℚ(√−d), h sesquilinear on V, h(v_i, v_j) = a_i δ_{ij} with a_i ∈ ℚ_{>0} and ∏ a_i ∈ (ℚ^×)² ⟹ ∃ e_1,…,e_r ∈ V with h(e_i, e_j) = δ_{ij}
a.known_as: Landherr's theorem that Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields are classified by rank, determinant modulo norms and signatures, here for a positive definite diagonal form with square determinant, which is therefore isometric to the unit form
a.reference: W. Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 11 (1936)
a.why: On the span of the v_i the form is the diagonal Hermitian form with positive coefficients and a square, hence norm, determinant, so Landherr's theorem gives an orthonormal basis there, while the kind is a judgement and the statement is word for word the same as Theorem 60.

b.states: Let K be a number field, V a K-vector space, σ a ring endomorphism of K and h a form on V that is K-linear in its first argument and σ-semilinear in its second. Assume d > 0 and θ in K satisfy θ² = −d and σ(θ) = −θ, and that every element of K equals a + bθ with rational a and b. Let v_1,…,v_r be vectors in V and a_1,…,a_r positive rationals with h(v_i, v_j) = a_i when i = j and 0 otherwise, and with ∏ a_i a square in ℚ. Then there are vectors e_1,…,e_r in V with h(e_i, e_j) = 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise.
b.known_as: Landherr's theorem classifying hermitian forms over number fields by rank, determinant modulo norms and signatures, applied to a positive definite diagonal form over an imaginary quadratic field

check.known_as: Landherr's theorem classifying Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields by rank, determinant modulo norms and signatures, here for a positive definite diagonal form over an imaginary quadratic field with square determinant
check.note: The form h is assumed neither Hermitian nor nondegenerate on V, which costs nothing because the vectors e_i can be found in the span of the v_i, where the Gram matrix of h is the positive diagonal matrix of the a_i.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_coboundary_of_fraction_cocycle_homogeneous_ideal
theorems.areas: ring theory

a.states: Let A be a Noetherian ring and J a homogeneous ideal of S = A[X_0,…,X_n]. Then there is d₀ such that for every d ≥ d₀ and every N, every family of forms F_{ij} of degree d + 2N for which X_l^N F_{ij} + X_i^N F_{jl} − X_j^N F_{il} lies in J after multiplication by a power of X_iX_jX_l is a Čech coboundary. That means there are N' and forms G_i of degree d + N' such that (X_iX_j)^{N'}F_{ij} − (X_iX_j)^N(X_j^{N'}G_i − X_i^{N'}G_j) lies in J after multiplication by a power of X_iX_j.
a.notation: ∃ d₀ ∀ d ≥ d₀, Ȟ¹({D(X_i)}, (S/J)~(d)) = 0 on P^n_A, with cochains written as fractions F_{ij}/(X_iX_j)^N
a.known_as: Serre's vanishing theorem, here for the first Čech cohomology of the twisted structure sheaf of a closed subscheme of P^n_A in the standard affine cover
a.reference: J.-P. Serre, Faisceaux algébriques cohérents, Annals of Mathematics 61 (1955)
a.why: The fractions F_{ij}/(X_iX_j)^N of degree d are exactly the Čech 1-cochains of (S/J)~(d) in the standard affine cover, which computes sheaf cohomology on the separated scheme P^n_A, so the statement is Serre vanishing for H¹ of this coherent sheaf.

b.states: For a Noetherian ring A, a natural number n and an ideal J of A[X_0,…,X_n] that contains every homogeneous component of each of its elements, there is d₀ with the following property for all d ≥ d₀ and all N. Let the forms F_{ij} have degree d + 2N, and let the fractions F_{ij}/(X_iX_j)^N satisfy the Čech cocycle identity modulo J after multiplication by a power of X_iX_jX_l. Then there are N' and forms G_i of degree d + N' such that F_{ij}/(X_iX_j)^N equals G_i/X_i^{N'} − G_j/X_j^{N'} modulo J after multiplication by a power of X_iX_j.
b.known_as: Serre's vanishing theorem, that H¹(Pⁿ_A, F(d)) = 0 for d large and F coherent, for the structure sheaf of the closed subscheme cut out by J and written with Čech cocycles of the standard cover

check.known_as: Serre's vanishing theorem, here for H¹ of the twists of the structure sheaf of the closed subscheme V(J) of Pⁿ_A, written with Čech cocycles of the standard affine cover
check.note: The fractions F_{ij}/(X_iX_j)^N with F_{ij} of degree d + 2N are the Čech 1-cochains of (S/J)~(d) for the standard affine cover, and the homogeneity hypothesis on J costs nothing because every element tested for membership in J is homogeneous.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.HermGlobal.exists_represent
theorems.areas: number fields

a.states: Let E/F be an extension of number fields with an F-automorphism σ of E such that σ∘σ is the identity and the elements fixed by σ are exactly the elements of F, and let θ ∈ E be nonzero with σ(θ) = −θ, which forces σ ≠ id and makes E/F quadratic. Let r ≥ 2, let g_1, …, g_r be nonzero elements of E fixed by σ and let b be a nonzero element of E fixed by σ, so that all of them lie in F. Assume that for every ring homomorphism τ from E to ℂ with τ∘σ equal to complex conjugation after τ there is an index i such that Re τ(g_i) > 0 holds exactly when Re τ(b) > 0, which says that b has the sign of some g_i at every real place of F that becomes complex in E. Then some z ∈ E^r satisfies Σ_i g_i z_i σ(z_i) = b, so the diagonal Hermitian form ⟨g_1, …, g_r⟩ represents b.
a.notation: σ² = id, E^σ = F, θ ≠ 0, σθ = −θ, r ≥ 2, g_i, b ∈ F^×, (∀ τ ∈ Hom(E, ℂ) with τ∘σ = conj∘τ ∃ i with (Re τ(g_i) > 0 ⇔ Re τ(b) > 0)) ⇒ ∃ z ∈ E^r with Σ_{i=1}^r g_i z_i σ(z_i) = b
a.known_as: Local–global principle for representations by Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields, a consequence of Landherr's theorem or of the Hasse–Minkowski theorem for the trace form, for a diagonal form of rank at least 2, where only the real places of F that ramify in E impose a condition
a.reference: W. Scharlau, Quadratic and Hermitian Forms, Springer, 1985, Chapter 10
a.why: The content is certainly the sufficiency half of the Hasse principle for Hermitian forms, but choosing weaker over special case depends on counting the dropped converse and the restriction to diagonal forms.

b.states: For number fields F and E with E an F-algebra, the theorem takes an F-automorphism σ of E with σ(σ(t)) = t whose fixed elements are exactly the image of F, a nonzero θ with σ(θ) = −θ (which forces σ to differ from the identity), a natural number r with 2 ≤ r, nonzero σ-fixed elements g_1, …, g_r and a nonzero σ-fixed element b. It assumes the following for every ring homomorphism τ from E to ℂ such that τ(σ(x)) is the complex conjugate of τ(x) for all x. Some index i then has Re τ(g_i) > 0 exactly when Re τ(b) > 0. The conclusion is that some z in E^r satisfies Σ_i z_i · g_i · σ(z_i) = b, so the diagonal Hermitian form with coefficients g_i represents b.
b.known_as: Landherr's Hasse principle for Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields, in its corollary that a Hermitian form of rank at least 2 represents every nonzero element of the base field whose sign matches a coefficient at each real place of F that becomes complex in E

check.known_as: The representation criterion for Hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields, a corollary of Landherr's Hasse principle (or of the Hasse–Minkowski theorem applied to the trace form), by which a Hermitian form of rank at least 2 represents a nonzero element of the base field exactly when that element has the sign of some diagonal coefficient at every real place of F that becomes complex in E
check.note: The Lean text lists no condition at the finite places and at the other infinite places because a Hermitian form of rank at least 2 represents every nonzero element there, which is why the hypothesis r ≥ 2 appears, and the dropped converse is elementary.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.adicCompletion_isDomain_and_isIntegrallyClosed
theorems.areas: ring theory

a.states: For every commutative ring A that is a local integral domain, integrally closed, of characteristic zero and essentially of finite type over ℤ, the completion of A with respect to its maximal ideal is again an integral domain and is integrally closed.
a.notation: A local normal domain, char A = 0, A essentially of finite type over ℤ ⇒ Â = lim A/𝔪^n is a normal domain
a.known_as: Analytic normality of excellent normal local rings, which is Zariski's theorem on analytic normality in the generality of Nagata and Grothendieck, applied to rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent
a.reference: A. Grothendieck, Éléments de géométrie algébrique IV, seconde partie, Publ. Math. IHÉS 24, 1965, (7.8.3)
a.why: The mathematical match is clear, but whether the result counts as a named theorem or as a textbook consequence of excellence is a judgement call.

b.states: Take any local domain A that is integrally closed, has characteristic zero and is essentially of finite type over ℤ. The completion of A with respect to its maximal ideal is then a domain, and it is integrally closed.
b.known_as: Zariski's theorem on analytic normality in the form of Grothendieck and Nagata, which says that the completion of a normal excellent local ring is normal (EGA IV 7.8.3), applied to rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent

check.known_as: Zariski's theorem on analytic normality in the form of Nagata and Grothendieck (EGA IV 7.8.3), by which the completion of an excellent normal local domain is a normal domain, applied to local rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent
check.note: The hypothesis of characteristic zero is not needed for the published theorem and only narrows the class of rings, while mixed-characteristic rings such as ℤ localized at a prime stay included.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.wp_isAlgebraic
theorems.areas: special functions, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let L be the lattice in ℂ of a period pair, with Weierstrass invariants g₂ and g₃ and Weierstrass function ℘_L, and let M be a subfield of ℂ that contains g₂ and g₃. If n > 0 and t ∈ ℂ satisfy n·t ∈ L and t ∉ L, then ℘_L(t) is algebraic over M.
a.notation: g₂(L), g₃(L) ∈ M ⊆ ℂ, n ≥ 1, nt ∈ L, t ∉ L ⇒ ℘_L(t) is algebraic over M
a.known_as: Algebraicity of the division values of the Weierstrass ℘-function, since ℘ at a nonzero n-torsion point is a root of the n-th division polynomial, whose coefficients lie in ℤ[g₂, g₃]
a.reference: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009, Exercise 3.7
a.why: The statement is the textbook fact that division values of ℘ are roots of division polynomials with coefficients in ℚ(g₂, g₃).

b.states: Let L be a period pair with lattice Λ and let M be a subfield of ℂ that contains the invariants g₂ and g₃ of L. Let n be a natural number with 0 < n, and let t be a complex number with n·t in Λ and t not in Λ. Then the Weierstrass value ℘_L(t) is algebraic over M.
b.known_as: the algebraicity of the division values of the Weierstrass ℘-function over ℚ(g₂, g₃), which follows from the division polynomials

check.known_as: The algebraicity of the division values of the Weierstrass ℘-function over ℚ(g₂, g₃), which follows from the division polynomials

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.ThetaNullNormSquares.jacobiTheta₂_eq_zero_iff
theorems.areas: modular forms, complex analysis

a.states: Let τ lie in the upper half-plane, let a ≠ 0 and let Λ be the additive subgroup a(ℤτ + ℤ) of ℂ. Then for every w ∈ ℂ the Jacobi theta function θ(z, τ) = Σ_{n∈ℤ} exp(2πinz + πin²τ) vanishes at z = w + (τ+1)/2 if and only if a·w ∈ Λ, which holds exactly when w ∈ ℤτ + ℤ.
a.known_as: Zeros of the Jacobi theta function, which vanishes exactly at the points (1+τ)/2 + ℤ + ℤτ
a.reference: D. Mumford, Tata Lectures on Theta I, Birkhäuser, 1983, Chapter I
a.why: Mathlib's jacobiTheta₂ is the classical θ(z, τ), and the scaling by a only rewrites the lattice ℤτ + ℤ.

b.states: Let τ lie in the upper half-plane, let a be a nonzero complex number and let Λ be the additive subgroup a·(ℤτ + ℤ) of ℂ. For every complex w, the Jacobi theta function θ(z, τ) = Σ_n exp(2πinz + πin²τ) vanishes at z = w + (τ + 1)/2 exactly when a·w lies in Λ, which is exactly when w lies in ℤτ + ℤ.
b.known_as: the location of the zeros of the Jacobi theta function, which vanishes exactly at the points (1 + τ)/2 + ℤ + ℤτ

check.known_as: The location of the zeros of the Jacobi theta function, which vanishes exactly at the points (τ + 1)/2 + ℤ + ℤτ
check.note: The parameters a and Λ add nothing to the content, since a·w ∈ Λ holds exactly when w ∈ ℤτ + ℤ.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.free_of_etale_on_punctured_spectrum
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, group theory

a.states: Let R be a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal is generated by as many elements as the Krull dimension of R, so that R is a regular local ring, and assume dim R ≥ 3. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite R-algebra on which R acts faithfully. If R_𝔭 ⊗_R A is étale over R_𝔭 for every prime 𝔭 of R other than the maximal ideal, then A is a free R-module.
a.notation: R regular local, dim R ≥ 3, R ↪ A finite, A normal domain, R_𝔭 → A_𝔭 étale for all 𝔭 ≠ 𝔪 ⇒ A ≅ R^n as R-modules
a.known_as: Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus, which makes A étale and hence free over R
a.reference: M. Nagata, On the purity of branch loci in regular local rings, Illinois J. Math. 3, 1959
a.why: The Lean text follows from purity with étale weakened to free and with the extra bound dim R ≥ 3, and that bound suggests a statement shaped for one proof route, which leaves the kind open.

b.states: Let R be a Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal needs exactly as many generators as the Krull dimension of R, so that R is a regular local ring, and assume that this dimension is at least 3. Let A be an integrally closed domain that is a finite R-algebra on which R acts faithfully. Suppose that for every prime p of R other than the maximal ideal, R_p ⊗_R A is étale over R_p. Then A is a free R-module.
b.known_as: the Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus for a finite normal extension of a regular local ring, which already in dimension at least 2 makes A étale and hence free over R

check.known_as: The Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus for a finite normal extension of a regular local ring, in dimension at least 3 and with étaleness assumed on the whole punctured spectrum
check.note: Under the hypotheses the conclusion that A is free is equivalent to étaleness, because the discriminant of a free A that is not a unit would lie in a height-one prime other than the maximal ideal, so the Lean text is the hard case of purity in dimension at least 3 and not a weakening of its conclusion.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.c_one_h2_units_subsingleton
theorems.areas: representation theory, linear algebra, ring theory, field theory, homological algebra

a.states: Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of fields. Assume that K has property C₁, which means that every homogeneous polynomial over K of degree d in n variables with 0 < d < n has a nonzero zero in K^n. Then the second cohomology group of Aut_K(L) with coefficients in the multiplicative group L^× has at most one element.
a.notation: L/K finite Galois, K is C₁ ⇒ H²(Gal(L/K), L^×) = 0
a.known_as: Vanishing of the Brauer group of a quasi-algebraically closed (C₁) field
a.reference: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, Springer, 1979, Chapter X, §7
a.why: Serre proves exactly that H²(Gal(L/K), L^×) vanishes for every finite Galois extension L of a C₁ field K, and the Lean hypothesis is the usual definition of C₁.

b.states: Let L be a finite Galois extension of a field K. Assume that K has property C₁, which means that every homogeneous polynomial over K of degree d in n variables with 0 < d < n has a nonzero zero in K^n. Then the second group cohomology of the K-automorphism group of L, acting on the multiplicative group of L, has at most one element.
b.known_as: the theorem that a quasi-algebraically closed (C₁) field has trivial Brauer group, stated for each relative Brauer group H²(Gal(L/K), L^×)

check.known_as: The vanishing of the Brauer group of a quasi-algebraically closed (C₁) field, stated for each relative Brauer group H²(Gal(L/K), L^×)
check.note: The Lean hypothesis is the usual definition of a C₁ field, which finite fields meet by the Chevalley–Warning theorem and function fields of curves over algebraically closed fields meet by Tsen's theorem.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_place_pow_and_not_pow'
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let p be a prime and F a totally complex number field that contains a primitive p-th root of unity. Let δ and u be nonzero elements of F such that δ is not a p-th power in F and u differs from δ^k r^p for every k ∈ ℕ and r ∈ F, so that δ and u are independent in F^×/F^{×p}, and let S₀ be a finite set of finite places of F. Then some finite place v outside S₀ has δ a p-th power in the completion F_v and u not a p-th power in F_v.
a.notation: ζ_p ∈ F, δ ∉ F^p, u ∉ δ^ℕ·F^p, S₀ finite ⇒ ∃ v ∉ S₀ with δ ∈ (F_v)^p and u ∉ (F_v)^p
a.known_as: Consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem for the Kummer extension F(δ^{1/p}, u^{1/p})/F, whose Galois group is (ℤ/p)²
a.reference: N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören, Math. Ann. 95, 1926
a.why: The proof by Kummer theory and Chebotarev is routine, but the pairing of one local p-th power with one local non-power is shaped for a particular use and is not a textbook statement.

b.states: Let p be a prime and let F be a totally complex number field that contains a primitive p-th root of unity ζ. Let δ and u be nonzero elements of F such that δ is not a p-th power in F and u differs from δ^k·r^p for every natural k and every r in F. Then for every finite set S₀ of finite places of F there is a finite place v outside S₀ at which δ is a p-th power in the completion F_v and u is not a p-th power in F_v.
b.known_as: the Chebotarev density theorem applied to the Kummer extension F(δ^{1/p}, u^{1/p})/F of degree p², whose Frobenius elements fix the p-th root of δ and move the p-th root of u at infinitely many places

check.known_as: A consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem for the Kummer extension F(δ^{1/p}, u^{1/p})/F, whose Galois group is (ℤ/pℤ)²
check.note: The hypothesis that F is totally complex follows from ζ ∈ F when p is odd and only narrows the fields when p = 2.

theorems.name: GroundTheory.Global.Elliptic.exists_le_forall_torsion_mem
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, linear algebra, field theory

a.states: Let K be a field with a ring map to ℂ, let L₀ be an intermediate field between K and ℂ that is finite over K, and let A be an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over L₀. For every m ≠ 0 there is an intermediate field M, finite over K and containing L₀, such that both coordinates of every affine point of A over ℂ that is killed by m lie in M.
a.notation: L₀/K finite, A/L₀ elliptic, m ≠ 0 ⇒ ∃ M ⊇ L₀ with M/K finite and x(P), y(P) ∈ M for every affine P ∈ A(ℂ) with mP = O
a.known_as: Finiteness of the m-division field L₀(A[m]) over L₀
a.reference: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009, Chapter VIII, §1
a.why: The statement is the familiar fact that adjoining the coordinates of the finitely many m-torsion points gives a finite extension.

b.states: Let K be a field with ℂ a K-algebra, let L₀ be an intermediate field between K and ℂ that is finite over K, let A be an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over L₀ and let m be a nonzero natural number. Then some intermediate field M between K and ℂ is finite over K, contains L₀ and contains both coordinates of every affine complex point (x, y) of A whose m-fold multiple is zero.
b.known_as: the finiteness of the m-torsion field L₀(A[m]) over the field of definition of an elliptic curve

check.known_as: The finiteness of the m-division field L₀(A[m]) of an elliptic curve over its field of definition

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.QNorm.exists_odd_order_at_even_elsewhere
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let F be a number field, δ ∈ F^× a non-square and σ₀ a real embedding of F. Assume a condition H, which says that every nonzero t ∈ F whose valuation is even at every finite place where δ is not a local square, and which is positive under every real embedding other than σ₀, is also positive under σ₀. Then for every finite place v₀ there is a nonzero t ∈ F with odd valuation at v₀ and even valuation at every other finite place where δ is not a local square.
a.notation: δ ∉ F^{×2}, σ₀ real, [∀ t ≠ 0, ((∀ v finite, δ ∈ (F_v)² ∨ 2 | v(t)) ∧ (∀ real σ ≠ σ₀, σ(t) > 0)) ⇒ σ₀(t) > 0] ⇒ ∀ v₀ ∃ t ≠ 0 with v₀(t) odd and (∀ v ≠ v₀, δ ∈ (F_v)² ∨ 2 | v(t))
a.known_as: no published result known, a parity lemma for valuations at the non-split places of the quadratic extension F(√δ)/F, whose hypothesis H acts as a sign condition of Hilbert reciprocity type
a.vacuity: The hypothesis H cannot be met when F has exactly one real embedding, since t = −1 violates it, nor whenever a unit is negative under σ₀ and positive under the other real embeddings, so the theorem says nothing for F = ℚ, and for a totally complex F no σ₀ exists, although H does hold for instance for F = ℚ(√3) and δ = −1 by Hilbert reciprocity.
a.why: I know no source that states this lemma, and its hypothesis H looks tailored to one argument.

b.states: Let F be a number field with a real embedding σ₀, and let δ be a nonzero element of F that is not a square. Assume the following about every nonzero t in F whose valuation is even at each finite place v where δ is not a square in the completion F_v. If such a t is positive at every real embedding other than σ₀, it is also positive at σ₀. Then every finite place v₀ has a nonzero t in F whose valuation is odd at v₀ and even at every other finite place where δ is not a square in the completion.
b.known_as: a consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem, because the hypothesis rules out that F(√δ) lies in the Hilbert class field of F, and the primes that split in such a quadratic extension then meet every ideal class
b.vacuity: The hypothesis fails at t = −1 whenever F has exactly one real embedding, and totally complex fields have no σ₀, so the statement has content only for fields with at least two real embeddings, where the hypothesis can hold, for example for F = ℚ(√3) and δ = −1.

check.known_as: No published result known, a lemma that finds an element with odd valuation at one given place and even valuation at the other places where δ is not a local square, under a sign hypothesis of Hilbert reciprocity type
check.vacuity: The hypothesis on t fails at t = −1 when F has exactly one real embedding and at any unit that is negative at σ₀ and positive at the other real embeddings, and a totally complex F has no σ₀, so the theorem is empty for such fields, although F = ℚ(√3) with δ = −1 meets the hypothesis by Hilbert reciprocity.
check.note: The statement is true because its hypothesis keeps F(√δ) out of the Hilbert class field of F, and the Chebotarev density theorem then puts primes that split in F(√δ) into every ideal class.

theorems.name: GroundTheory.Global.Elliptic.isAlgebraic_of_nsmul_eq_zero
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, ring theory

a.states: Let F be a field with a ring map to ℂ and A an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over F. If m ≠ 0 and (x, y) is a nonsingular affine point of A over ℂ whose m-th multiple is the identity in the group of points, then x and y are algebraic over F.
a.notation: A/F elliptic, F → ℂ, m ≠ 0, P = (x, y) ∈ A(ℂ), mP = O ⇒ x and y are algebraic over F
a.known_as: Torsion points of an elliptic curve have algebraic coordinates, A[m] ⊆ A(F̄), as the division polynomials show
a.reference: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009, Exercise 3.7
a.why: The statement is the textbook fact that the m-torsion over ℂ already lies over the algebraic closure of the base field.

b.states: Let F be a field with ℂ an F-algebra, and let A be an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over F. Suppose that (x, y) is an affine point of A over ℂ and that m·(x, y) = 0 for a nonzero natural number m. Then x and y are both algebraic over F.
b.known_as: the algebraicity of the coordinates of torsion points of an elliptic curve over its field of definition, through the division polynomials

check.known_as: The algebraicity of the coordinates of the torsion points of an elliptic curve over its field of definition, through the division polynomials

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_prime_absNorm_eq_of_irreducible_cyclotomic'
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let K be a number field and m a prime such that the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_m is irreducible over K. Then for every unit τ of ℤ/mℤ and every finite set S of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K there is a nonzero prime P outside S whose absolute norm N(P) is a rational prime congruent to τ modulo m.
a.notation: Φ_m irreducible over K, τ ∈ (ℤ/m)^×, S finite ⇒ ∃ P ∉ S with N(P) prime and N(P) ≡ τ (mod m)
a.known_as: Chebotarev density theorem for the cyclotomic extension K(ζ_m)/K, whose Galois group is all of (ℤ/m)^× because Φ_m is irreducible, combined with the fact that primes of degree one have density one
a.reference: J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Springer, 1999, Chapter VII, Theorem 13.4
a.why: The derivation from Chebotarev is a routine exercise, so the relation is certain, while the line between standard fact and technical step is less sharp.

b.states: Let K be a number field and m a prime such that the m-th cyclotomic polynomial is irreducible over K. Then for every unit τ of ℤ/mℤ and every finite set S of nonzero primes of the ring of integers of K, some prime P outside S has an absolute norm that is a rational prime congruent to τ modulo m.
b.known_as: the Chebotarev density theorem for the cyclotomic extension K(ζ_m)/K, which is Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions for primes of degree one in a number field

check.known_as: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions for primes of degree one in a number field, which is the Chebotarev density theorem for K(ζ_m)/K combined with the density one of primes of degree one
check.note: For K = ℚ the statement is Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions to a prime modulus.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_place_not_pow_adicCompletion
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let p be a prime and F a totally complex number field that contains a primitive p-th root of unity. If u ∈ F is nonzero and not a p-th power in F, then for every finite set S₀ of finite places of F there is a finite place v outside S₀ such that u is not a p-th power in the completion F_v.
a.notation: ζ_p ∈ F, u ∈ F^× ∖ F^{×p}, S₀ finite ⇒ ∃ v ∉ S₀ with u ∉ (F_v)^p
a.known_as: Local–global principle for p-th powers, the prime-exponent case of the Grunwald–Wang theorem, which says that an element that is a p-th power at almost all places is a p-th power in F
a.reference: E. Artin and J. Tate, Class Field Theory, Benjamin, 1968, Chapter X
a.why: The match with the prime-exponent case is exact, and only the choice of kind is uncertain because the general result carries the name Grunwald–Wang.

b.states: Let p be a prime and let F be a totally complex number field that contains a primitive p-th root of unity ζ. Let u be a nonzero element of F that is not a p-th power in F. Then for every finite set S₀ of finite places of F there is a finite place v outside S₀ such that u is not a p-th power in the completion F_v.
b.known_as: the local–global principle for p-th powers, by which an element that is a p-th power in almost all completions is a p-th power (the case of a prime exponent in the Grunwald–Wang theorem, or a corollary of the Chebotarev density theorem)

check.known_as: The local–global principle for p-th powers, by which an element that is a p-th power in almost all completions is a p-th power, here in the case where F contains the p-th roots of unity, which is the prime-exponent case of the Grunwald–Wang theorem
check.note: The hypothesis that F is totally complex follows from ζ ∈ F when p is odd.

theorems.name: GroundTheory.Arith.Abelian.finite_torsionBy_natCast
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, field theory

a.states: Let F be an algebraically closed field and E an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over F. For every natural number n ≠ 0 the subgroup of points P ∈ E(F) with nP = O is finite. The prime p and the assumption that F has characteristic p appear in the variable lines but are omitted from this theorem, so the field may have any characteristic.
a.notation: F algebraically closed, E/F elliptic, n ≥ 1 ⇒ E(F)[n] is finite
a.known_as: Structure of the n-torsion of an elliptic curve, E[n] ≅ (ℤ/n)² when the characteristic does not divide n and E[p^e] ≅ 0 or ℤ/p^e in characteristic p
a.reference: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009, Corollary III.6.4
a.why: Silverman's corollary gives the exact group structure, and the Lean text keeps only its finiteness.

b.states: Let F be an algebraically closed field and E an elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over F. For every nonzero natural number n, the subgroup of points P of E over F with n·P = 0 is finite. The statement omits the prime p and the hypothesis on the characteristic of F, so it assumes no condition on the characteristic.
b.known_as: the finiteness of the n-torsion subgroup E[n] of an elliptic curve, which has at most n² elements

check.known_as: The finiteness of the n-torsion subgroup E[n] of an elliptic curve, which has at most n² elements and is isomorphic to (ℤ/nℤ)² when the characteristic does not divide n

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.elliptic_points_stabilizer
theorems.areas: modular forms, complex analysis, linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: For every τ₀ in the upper half-plane two implications hold. If the Eisenstein series E₆ vanishes at τ₀, then some u = (a b, c d) ∈ SL(2, ℤ) fixes τ₀ and its automorphy factor cτ₀ + d is a primitive fourth root of unity. If E₄ vanishes at τ₀, then some u ∈ SL(2, ℤ) fixes τ₀ and cτ₀ + d is a primitive sixth root of unity.
a.notation: ∀ τ₀ ∈ ℍ, (E₆(τ₀) = 0 ⇒ ∃ u ∈ SL₂(ℤ), uτ₀ = τ₀ and cτ₀ + d ∈ μ₄ primitive) ∧ (E₄(τ₀) = 0 ⇒ ∃ u ∈ SL₂(ℤ), uτ₀ = τ₀ and cτ₀ + d ∈ μ₆ primitive)
a.known_as: Zeros of E₄ and E₆ by the valence formula, E₆ vanishing only on the SL₂(ℤ)-orbit of i and E₄ only on the orbit of ρ = e^{2πi/3}, together with the stabilizers of these elliptic points
a.reference: J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Springer, 1973, Chapter VII, §3
a.why: The Lean text follows at once from the location of the zeros and the stabilizers of i and ρ, and it keeps only the stabilizer information.

b.states: Every τ₀ in the upper half-plane satisfies two implications. If the Eisenstein series E₆ vanishes at τ₀, then some matrix u in SL(2, ℤ) fixes τ₀ and its automorphy factor cτ₀ + d is a primitive 4th root of unity. If E₄ vanishes at τ₀, then some u in SL(2, ℤ) fixes τ₀ and cτ₀ + d is a primitive 6th root of unity.
b.known_as: the location of the zeros of E₄ and E₆, which by the valence formula lie only on the orbits of ρ = e^{2πi/3} and of i, combined with the stabilizers of these elliptic points in SL(2, ℤ)

check.known_as: The location of the zeros of E₄ and E₆, which by the valence formula lie only on the SL(2, ℤ)-orbits of ρ = e^{2πi/3} and of i, together with the stabilizers of these elliptic points
check.note: The conclusion says only that a zero of E₆ has a stabilizer element with automorphy factor of order 4 and a zero of E₄ one with automorphy factor of order 6, and it gives neither the converse nor the simplicity of the zeros.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.EtaleCompletionRadical.isReduced_adicCompletion_tensor_residueField
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, group theory

a.states: Let A be a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ and P a prime ideal of A. Then the formal fibre Â ⊗_A κ(P) is a reduced ring, where Â is the completion of A at its maximal ideal and κ(P) is the residue field of P.
a.notation: A local and essentially of finite type over ℤ, P ∈ Spec A ⇒ Â ⊗_A κ(P) is reduced
a.known_as: Reducedness of the formal fibres of an excellent local ring, which are even geometrically regular, together with Grothendieck's theorem that rings essentially of finite type over ℤ are excellent
a.reference: A. Grothendieck, Éléments de géométrie algébrique IV, seconde partie, Publ. Math. IHÉS 24, 1965, (7.8.3)
a.why: Excellence gives geometrically regular formal fibres, and the Lean text claims only that they are reduced.

b.states: Let A be a local ring that is essentially of finite type over ℤ, and let P be a prime ideal of A. Then the tensor product over A of the completion of A at its maximal ideal with the residue field of P is a reduced ring. In other words, the formal fibre of A over P is reduced.
b.known_as: the excellence of rings essentially of finite type over ℤ (Grothendieck, EGA IV 7.8.3), whose formal fibres are geometrically regular and hence reduced

check.known_as: The reducedness of the formal fibres of an excellent local ring, whose formal fibres are geometrically regular, applied to local rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent by Grothendieck (EGA IV 7.8.3)
check.note: The Lean text assumes neither that A is a domain nor that A is Noetherian, since essential finite type over ℤ already makes A Noetherian.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.isOpen_identityComponents_smooth_groupScheme
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, topology, homological algebra, geometry

a.states: Let S be a scheme and G a group scheme over S whose structure morphism π from G to S is smooth. For a point x of G write s = π(x) and e(s) for the image of s under the unit section. Then the set of points x that lie in the connected component of the topological fibre π⁻¹(s) containing e(s), which is the union G⁰ of the identity components of the fibres, is open in G.
a.notation: G → S smooth group scheme ⇒ G⁰ = {x ∈ G | x lies in the connected component of π⁻¹(π(x)) that contains e(π(x))} is open in G
a.known_as: Openness of the identity component G⁰ of a smooth group scheme
a.reference: M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, Schémas en groupes I (SGA 3), Lecture Notes in Math. 151, Springer, 1970, Exposé VI_B, Théorème 3.10
a.why: The topological fibre of a morphism of schemes is homeomorphic to the scheme-theoretic fibre, so the Lean set is exactly G⁰ of SGA 3.

b.states: Let S be a scheme and G a group object in the category of schemes over S whose structure morphism is smooth. Consider the points x of G that lie in the connected component of their own fibre, the fibre over s = image of x, that contains the identity point e(s). The set of these points is open in G.
b.known_as: the openness of the identity component G⁰ of a smooth group scheme (SGA 3, exposé VI_B, 3.10)

check.known_as: The openness of the identity component G⁰ of a smooth group scheme (SGA 3, Exposé VI_B, 3.10)
check.note: The fibre in the Lean text is the topological subspace π⁻¹(s) of G, which is homeomorphic to the underlying space of the scheme-theoretic fibre G_s, so the set is the usual G⁰.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.TorsionZero.card_zeros_le_of_growth
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K be algebraically closed and R an ℕ-graded K-algebra that is a domain, with elements x_1, …, x_m of degree N ≥ 1 such that every element of degree Ne times a power of each x_i is a homogeneous polynomial of matching degree in the x_j, and with dim_K R_{Ne} ≤ (Be)^g for all e ≥ 1, where g ≥ 1 is the Krull dimension of the coordinate ring C of the variety X of the x_j in the affine chart x_{i₀} ≠ 0. A set Pt of K-points of R is mapped bijectively onto the points of X by the projective coordinates (x_1(p) : … : x_m(p)). Let s ≠ 0 have degree Nd, let finitely many f_j have degree Na, and assume the common zero set Z of the f_j in Pt is finite. Then at most B^g · g! · d · a^{g−1} points of Z are zeros of s.
a.notation: #{p ∈ Z | s(p) = 0} ≤ B^g · g! · d · a^{g−1}, where Z = V(f_j) ⊆ X is finite, dim X = g, dim R_{Ne} ≤ (Be)^g, s ∈ R_{Nd} ∖ {0} and f_j ∈ R_{Na}
a.known_as: Bézout-type bound for isolated common zeros of sections on a projective variety, namely the refined Bézout inequality combined with the bound deg X ≤ g!·B^g that the Hilbert-function estimate gives
a.reference: W. Fulton, Intersection Theory, Springer, 1984, Example 8.4.6
a.why: The kind is clear from the bespoke encoding of the variety through a graded ring and a set of points, but the relation to the refined Bézout inequality is only approximate because the Lean text also builds in a degree bound from the Hilbert function.

b.states: Let K be an algebraically closed field and R a K-algebra domain with an ℕ-grading 𝒜, and assume g ≥ 1, N ≥ 1 and dim 𝒜(Ne) ≤ (Be)^g for every e ≥ 1. Let x_1, …, x_m be elements of degree N such that any element of degree Ne, times a suitable power of any x_i, is a homogeneous polynomial in the x_j. A domain C of Krull dimension g, generated by elements r_j with r_{i₀} = 1 and x_{i₀} ≠ 0, has the same homogeneous relations as the x_j, and a type of points, each with a K-algebra evaluation of R, corresponds one to one through the ratios of the values of the x_j with the K-points of the projective variety those relations define. If s ≠ 0 has degree Nd and Z is a finite set of points that is exactly the common zero set of finitely many elements of degree Na, then at most B^g · g! · d · a^(g − 1) points of Z are zeros of s.
b.known_as: a Bézout-type bound, the refined Bézout inequality (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Example 8.4.6) for a projective variety of dimension g whose degree is at most B^g · g! by the growth of its Hilbert function

check.known_as: A Bézout-type bound, the refined Bézout inequality (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Example 8.4.6) for a projective variety of dimension g whose degree is at most g!·B^g by the growth of its Hilbert function
check.note: The variety and its points are encoded through a graded domain, a ring C and a type of evaluation maps, and C turns out to be the coordinate ring of the chart x_{i₀} ≠ 0 of the projective variety that the homogeneous relations of the x_j define, because a relation of C homogenized in the variable of index i₀ is a homogeneous relation of the x_j.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_idele_ne_algebraMap_mul_norm_of_not_isSquare
theorems.areas: number fields

a.states: Let F be a number field and δ ∈ F a non-square. Then there is an idele a of F with a ≠ t·(x² − δy²) for every t ∈ F and all adeles x and y of F. Since x² − δy² is the norm from the adeles of E = F(√δ), and an idele of this form forces t ≠ 0 and makes x + y√δ an idele of E, the statement says that F^× · N_{E/F}(𝔸_E^×) is a proper subgroup of 𝔸_F^×.
a.notation: δ ∉ F² ⇒ ∃ a ∈ 𝔸_F^× ∀ t ∈ F ∀ x, y ∈ 𝔸_F, a ≠ t(x² − δy²)
a.known_as: First fundamental inequality of global class field theory, by which the index of the norm group N_{E/F} C_E in the idele class group C_F is at least the degree of a cyclic extension E/F, here for a quadratic extension where it says that the index exceeds 1
a.reference: J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Springer, 1999, Chapter VI, §4
a.why: For a quadratic extension an index of at least 2 is the same as an index different from 1, so the match is exact, but some textbooks swap the names of the first and second inequality.

b.states: Let F be a number field and δ an element of F that is not a square. Then F has an idele a that differs from t·(x² − δy²) for every t in F and all adeles x and y of F. Hence a lies outside F^× times the norms from the ideles of F(√δ).
b.known_as: the first fundamental inequality of global class field theory, by which the idele norm index of F(√δ)/F is at least 2, which for a quadratic extension also follows from the Hilbert reciprocity law

check.known_as: The first fundamental inequality of global class field theory for the quadratic extension F(√δ)/F, by which the norm index in the idele class group is at least 2
check.note: Some textbooks call this inequality the second one, because the naming of the two fundamental inequalities varies.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.smoothAffineCurve_divisor_unit_decomposition
theorems.areas: ring theory, field theory, group theory

a.states: Let k be algebraically closed, let B be a Dedekind domain that is a finitely generated k-algebra, as the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve is, and let q be a natural number invertible in k. For all nonzero f and b in B and every m ∈ ℕ there are a nonzero g ∈ B comaximal with f, a unit u of B[1/(fg)] and elements n, d, t, n′, d′ of B, with n and d comaximal with f and with n′ and d′ comaximal with g, such that bd = u·n·f^m and u·t^q·d′ = n′ hold in B[1/(fg)]. In terms of divisors, u has order ord(b) − m·ord(f) at each zero of f and an order divisible by q at each zero of g.
a.notation: ∀ f, b ∈ B ∖ {0}, ∀ m ∈ ℕ, ∃ g ≠ 0 with (f, g) = B, ∃ u ∈ B_{fg}^×, ∃ n, d, t, n′, d′ ∈ B with (f, n) = (f, d) = (g, n′) = (g, d′) = B, bd = u·n·f^m and u·t^q·d′ = n′ in B_{fg}
a.known_as: no published result known, a technical lemma that prescribes the divisor of a unit on a smooth affine curve modulo q-th powers and rests on the divisibility of the Picard group of such a curve over an algebraically closed field
a.why: The statement is clearly a bespoke tool whose content reduces to the divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve, and I know no source that states it in this form.

b.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field, B a Dedekind domain finitely generated as a k-algebra and q a natural number invertible in k. Take any nonzero f and b in B and any natural m. Then there are a nonzero g coprime to f, a unit u of B[1/(fg)] and elements n, d, t, n', d' of B, with n and d coprime to f and n' and d' coprime to g, such that b·d = u·n·f^m and u·t^q·d' = n' in B[1/(fg)]. In terms of divisors, u has zeros and poles only above f and g, matches the order of b·f^(−m) at each prime above f, and has order at each prime above g equal to a multiple of q that is at most 0.
b.known_as: a consequence of the divisibility of the divisor class group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which is a quotient of the points of the Jacobian, together with the moving lemma for ideal classes

check.known_as: No published result known, a lemma that prescribes the divisor of a unit on a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field modulo q-th powers and rests on the divisibility of the Picard group of such a curve
check.note: The order of u at each prime above g equals −q times the order of t there, so it is a multiple of q that is at most 0.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.weber_values_congruences_mod_degree_one_prime
theorems.areas: number fields, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K ⊆ ℂ be an imaginary quadratic field, let L be a period pair whose lattice is 𝓞_K, let W be a valuation ring of ℂ, and let π ∈ 𝓞_K lie in the maximal ideal 𝔪_W and have ideal norm a prime p ≥ 5. Write Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃², j′ = g₂³/Δ, which equals j(𝓞_K)/1728, and h(t) = g₂g₃℘(t)/Δ for the Weber function. Then j′ ∈ W and j′ ≡ j′^p modulo 𝔪_W, and for every m not divisible by p and every t with mt ∈ L and t ∉ L the value h(t) lies in W and h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p modulo 𝔪_W. If moreover j′ and j′ − 1 are units of W, then h(t) ≡ h(t′) modulo 𝔪_W for two such points t and t′ forces t − t′ ∈ L or t + t′ ∈ L.
a.notation: Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃², j′ = g₂³/Δ, h(t) = g₂g₃℘(t)/Δ ⇒ j′ ∈ W, j′ ≡ j′^p (mod 𝔪_W), and ∀ m with p ∤ m ∀ t ∈ m⁻¹L ∖ L, h(t) ∈ W and h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p (mod 𝔪_W), and if j′, j′ − 1 ∈ W^× then h(t) ≡ h(t′) (mod 𝔪_W) ⇒ t ≡ ±t′ (mod L)
a.known_as: Congruence relations of Kronecker and Hasse for the singular modulus j(𝓞_K) and for the Weber function at torsion points, used in the proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication, here for a principal prime of degree one
a.reference: J. H. Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Springer, 1994, Chapter II
a.why: Each of the four claims is a textbook step of Hasse's proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication, but the bundle for the lattice 𝓞_K and a principal prime of degree one is the project's own, so the line between standard fact and technical step is uncertain.

b.states: Let K be an imaginary quadratic subfield of ℂ and L a period pair whose lattice is the ring of integers of K. Let W be a valuation subring of ℂ, let p be a prime with 5 ≤ p, and let π be an integer of K whose principal ideal has norm p and which lies in the maximal ideal of W. With J = g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) = j/1728 and the Weber function h(t) = g₂g₃/(g₂³ − 27g₃²)·℘(t), the conclusion is that J lies in W with J ≡ J^p modulo the maximal ideal of W, and that for every natural m not divisible by p and every t with m·t in the lattice and t outside it, h(t) lies in W and h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p. If moreover J and J − 1 are units of W, then any two such m-torsion points t and t' with h(t) ≡ h(t') satisfy t − t' or t + t' in the lattice.
b.known_as: Hasse's congruences for singular moduli and Weber function values at a prime of degree one (the Kronecker congruence relation, by which multiplication by π reduces to the p-th power Frobenius), the key step in Hasse's proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication

check.known_as: Hasse's congruences for the singular modulus j(𝓞_K) and for the Weber function at torsion points modulo a principal prime of degree one (the Kronecker congruence relation), together with the injectivity of reduction on prime-to-p torsion up to sign, the steps of Hasse's proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication
check.vacuity: For K = ℚ(i) and K = ℚ(√−3) one of g₃ and g₂ vanishes, so h is identically zero and J equals 1 or 0, which makes the congruences immediate and the premise of the last clause impossible, and the statement has content only for the other imaginary quadratic fields.
check.note: The statement bundles four claims for the lattice 𝓞_K and a principal prime of degree one, and the last claim needs J and J − 1 to be units, which excludes j ≡ 0 and j ≡ 1728 modulo the prime.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.WeberCongruence.weber_congruences
theorems.areas: number fields, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K be a subfield of ℂ that is an imaginary quadratic number field, let L be a lattice in ℂ equal to the ring of integers 𝒪_K, let W be any valuation ring of ℂ, and let π ∈ 𝒪_K generate an ideal of norm a prime p ≥ 5 and lie in the maximal ideal of W. Then J = g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²), which is j(L)/1728, lies in W and satisfies J ≡ J^p modulo the maximal ideal of W. For every odd m not divisible by p and every t with mt ∈ L and t ∉ L, the Weber value h(t) = (g₂g₃/(g₂³ − 27g₃²))·℘(t) lies in W and h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p modulo the maximal ideal. If J and J − 1 are also units of W, then two such m-division points t and t′ with h(t) ≡ h(t′) satisfy t ≡ t′ or t ≡ −t′ modulo L.
a.notation: K ⊂ ℂ imaginary quadratic, Λ = 𝒪_K, π ∈ 𝒪_K ∩ 𝔪_W, N(π) = p ≥ 5 prime, Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃², J = g₂³/Δ ⇒ J ∈ W, J ≡ J^p mod 𝔪_W, and for all odd m with p ∤ m and all t ∈ m⁻¹Λ ∖ Λ, h(t) = (g₂g₃/Δ)℘(t) ∈ W, h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p mod 𝔪_W, and (J, J − 1 ∉ 𝔪_W ∧ h(t) ≡ h(t′) mod 𝔪_W ⇒ t ≡ ±t′ mod Λ)
a.known_as: Hasse's congruences for the j-invariant and the Weber function of a lattice with complex multiplication by 𝒪_K at a principal prime of degree one, together with the injectivity of the reduced Weber function on m-division points up to sign, which are the inputs of the Weber–Hasse proof that these values generate class fields of K
a.reference: Goro Shimura, Introduction to the Arithmetic Theory of Automorphic Functions, 1971, Chapter 5
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by K = ℚ(i), π = 2 + i and p = 5, but for K = ℚ(i) and K = ℚ(√−3) the Weber function vanishes identically and the last clause has an unmet premise, so the clauses on h carry content only for the other imaginary quadratic fields.
a.why: Each clause matches a textbook congruence, but the bundling with the lattice 𝒪_K, a principal prime and odd m is tailored to one proof, so the line between standard fact and technical step is a judgement.

b.states: Take an imaginary quadratic subfield K of ℂ (a totally complex number field of degree 2 over ℚ), a period pair L whose lattice is the image of 𝓞_K, a valuation subring W of ℂ, an element π of 𝓞_K and a prime p ≥ 5 such that the ideal (π) has absolute norm p and π lies in the maximal ideal of W. Then J = g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) lies in W and J − J^p lies in the maximal ideal of W. Now take an odd m that p does not divide and any t with mt in the lattice and t outside it. Then h(t) = g₂g₃/(g₂³ − 27g₃²)·℘(t) lies in W, h(πt) − h(t)^p lies in the maximal ideal, and if J and J − 1 both lie outside the maximal ideal, two such points t and t' with h(t) − h(t') in the maximal ideal have t − t' or t + t' in the lattice.
b.known_as: the Kronecker congruence j^p ≡ j and Hasse's congruence h(πt) ≡ h(t)^p for the Weber function modulo a prime above a principal prime of degree one, together with the injectivity of reduction on prime-to-p torsion up to sign, as used in the proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication
b.vacuity: None found, but for K = ℚ(i) and K = ℚ(√−3) the function h is identically zero, so the Weber congruence is trivial there and the hypotheses of the last claim fail.

check.known_as: Hasse's congruence for the Weber function and the Kronecker congruence for the j-invariant of the lattice 𝒪_K at a principal prime of degree one, together with the injectivity up to sign of the reduced Weber function on division points of order prime to p, as used in the proof of the main theorem of complex multiplication
check.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by K = ℚ(i), π = 2 + i and p = 5, but for K = ℚ(i) and K = ℚ(√−3) the function h vanishes identically and the premise of the last clause fails, so the clauses on h have content only for the other imaginary quadratic fields.
check.note: The valuation ring W ranges over all valuation subrings of ℂ, and the hypothesis that π lies in its maximal ideal forces W to lie over the prime (π), while the statement covers only the lattice 𝒪_K itself and odd orders m.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.j_invariant_equal_sl2_orbit
theorems.areas: modular forms, complex analysis, linear algebra

a.states: For all points τ and σ of the upper half-plane, if E₄(τ)³E₆(σ)² = E₆(τ)²E₄(σ)³, where E₄ and E₆ are the Eisenstein series of weights 4 and 6, then some matrix γ in SL₂(ℤ) satisfies τ = γσ under the Möbius action. E₄³ and E₆² never vanish together on the upper half-plane, so the hypothesis is equivalent to j(τ) = j(σ), and it does not change when E₄ and E₆ are rescaled.
a.notation: ∀ τ, σ ∈ ℍ, E₄(τ)³E₆(σ)² = E₆(τ)²E₄(σ)³ ⇒ ∃ γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), τ = γ·σ
a.known_as: injectivity of the modular j-function on SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ, one half of the theorem that j induces a bijection from SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ onto ℂ
a.reference: Jean-Pierre Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, 1973, Chapter VII, Proposition 5
a.why: The hypothesis is the equation j(τ) = j(σ) with the denominators cleared, and the injectivity of j on the orbit space is a textbook proposition whose surjectivity half is omitted here.

b.states: For all τ and σ in the upper half-plane, if E₄(τ)³E₆(σ)² = E₆(τ)²E₄(σ)³, then τ = γ·σ for some γ in SL(2, ℤ). The discriminant does not vanish on the upper half-plane, so the hypothesis is equivalent to j(τ) = j(σ).
b.known_as: the injectivity of the modular j-invariant on SL(2, ℤ)\ℍ, which is one half of the theorem that j induces a bijection from SL(2, ℤ)\ℍ onto ℂ (Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Chapter VII)

check.known_as: injectivity of the modular j-invariant on SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ, one half of the theorem that j induces a bijection from SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ onto ℂ
check.note: The hypothesis is the equation j(τ) = j(σ) with the denominators cleared, which is equivalent to it because E₄³ − E₆² never vanishes on ℍ, and it does not depend on the normalisation of E₄ and E₆ because both sides scale by the same factor.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.exists_strictHenselisation
theorems.areas: ring theory, field theory, group theory

a.states: For every local ring R with residue field k and every separable closure Ω of k, there is a henselian local R-algebra S with local structure map whose residue field is separably closed and isomorphic to Ω as a k-algebra. Moreover S is flat over R, and the maximal ideal of R generates the maximal ideal of S. Finally S is the union of a nonempty directed family of R-subalgebras, each isomorphic as an R-algebra to the localization of some étale R-algebra at a prime ideal.
a.notation: ∀ (R, 𝔪, k) local, ∀ Ω = k^sep, ∃ S strictly henselian local, R → S local and flat, 𝔪S = 𝔪_S, κ(S) ≅_k Ω, S = ⋃_{i ∈ I} S_i with I directed and S_i ≅_R (A_i)_{𝔮_i}, A_i étale over R
a.known_as: existence of the strict henselization R^sh of a local ring, together with its standard properties
a.reference: Michel Raynaud, Anneaux locaux henséliens, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 169, 1970
a.why: The listed properties are those of the strict henselization, while the universal property that characterises it is left out, which makes the relation weaker and the choice of kind a judgement.

b.states: For every local ring R and every separable closure Ω of its residue field, there is an R-algebra S with the following properties. S is a Henselian local ring, the structure map is local and flat, the maximal ideal of R generates the maximal ideal of S, and the residue field of S is separably closed and isomorphic to Ω over the residue field of R. In addition, S is the union of a monotone family of R-subalgebras indexed by a nonempty directed preorder, and each member is isomorphic as an R-algebra to the localization of some étale R-algebra at some prime ideal.
b.known_as: the existence of the strict henselization of a local ring (EGA IV 18.8, Stacks Project)

check.known_as: existence of the strict henselization of a local ring with its standard properties (EGA IV 18.8, Stacks Project)
check.note: The universal property of the strict henselization is absent, and the primes q of the étale algebras need not lie over the maximal ideal of R, so the statement asserts the existence of a ring with these properties and not that S is unique.

theorems.name: UpperTheory.Kd.K4.nsAbs
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, field theory, group theory

a.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, K a finite extension of the rational function field k(X), and K′ a finite Galois extension of K, with k[X] mapping compatibly into both. Let m > 0 and let f ∈ K be nonzero such that at every valuation ring B of K containing k[X], f equals a unit of B times an m-th power. Then some nonzero f′ ∈ K′ has norm N_{K′/K}(f′) = f and has the same property at every valuation ring of K′ containing k[X]. In terms of divisors on the affine curves over the X-line, a function whose affine divisor is divisible by m is the norm of a function on the Galois cover whose affine divisor is again divisible by m.
a.notation: f ∈ K^×, div_C(f) ∈ m·Div(C) ⇒ ∃ f′ ∈ K′^×, N_{K′/K}(f′) = f and div_{C′}(f′) ∈ m·Div(C′), where C and C′ are the normalizations of the affine X-line in K and K′
a.known_as: no published result known, a norm-lifting statement along a finite Galois cover of curves for functions whose divisor on the affine part is divisible by m, which refines the surjectivity of the norm that Tsen's theorem gives
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by f = 1, and the conclusion does not follow at once because one f′ must satisfy the norm condition and the divisibility condition together.
a.why: The valuation-ring formulation and the shared exponent m show that the statement is shaped for one use, and I know no source that states this combination.

b.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, K a finite extension of k(X) that is compatible with k[X], and K' a finite Galois extension of K on which k[X] acts compatibly. Let m > 0 and let f be a nonzero element of K that, at every valuation subring of K containing k[X], equals a unit times an m-th power. Then there is a nonzero f' in K' with N_{K'/K}(f') = f that has the same property at every valuation subring of K' containing k[X].
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: no published result known, a norm-lifting statement along a finite Galois extension of function fields of curves for functions whose divisor on the affine part is divisible by m
check.note: The valuation rings of K that contain k[X] are K itself and the local rings at the closed points of the normalisation of the X-line in K, so the hypothesis says that the divisor of f on that affine curve is divisible by m.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.QNorm.exists_place_isSquare_and_not_isSquare
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let F be a number field, let δ and u be nonzero elements such that none of δ, u and uδ is a square in F, and let S₀ be a finite set of nonzero primes of the ring of integers. Then some nonzero prime v outside S₀ makes δ a square in the completion F_v while u is not a square in F_v.
a.notation: δ, u, uδ ∉ F^{×2}, S₀ finite ⇒ ∃ finite place v ∉ S₀ with δ ∈ F_v^{×2} and u ∉ F_v^{×2}
a.known_as: consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem for the biquadratic extension F(√δ, √u), whose Galois group is (ℤ/2)², applied to the element that fixes √δ and moves √u
a.reference: Jürgen Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, 1999, Chapter VII, Theorem 13.4
a.vacuity: The hypotheses δ ≠ 0 and u ≠ 0 are redundant because 0 is a square, and the remaining hypotheses can be met, for example by F = ℚ, δ = 2 and u = 3.
a.why: The derivation from Chebotarev's theorem is short and standard, but this two-element form is the shape of a lemma and not of a named result.

b.states: Let F be a number field, δ and u nonzero elements of F and S₀ a finite set of finite places. If δ, u and uδ are all non-squares in F, then at some finite place v outside S₀ the image of δ is a square in the completion F_v and the image of u is not.
b.known_as: a consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem for the biquadratic extension F(√δ, √u)/F, which gives infinitely many primes that split in F(√δ) and do not split in F(√u)
b.vacuity: The hypotheses δ ≠ 0 and u ≠ 0 are redundant because 0 is a square, but no hypothesis is impossible to meet.

check.known_as: a corollary of the Chebotarev density theorem for the biquadratic extension F(√δ, √u)/F, applied to the Frobenius class that fixes √δ and moves √u
check.vacuity: The hypotheses δ ≠ 0 and u ≠ 0 are redundant because 0 is a square, and the remaining hypotheses can be met, for example by F = ℚ, δ = 2 and u = 3.
check.note: The hypothesis that uδ is not a square makes F(√δ, √u) an extension of degree 4 with Galois group (ℤ/2)², which is what the Chebotarev argument needs.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.classGroup_dedekind_algClosed_divisible
theorems.areas: ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field and B a Dedekind domain that is a finitely generated k-algebra, which makes B the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve over k or k itself. For every natural number q whose image in k is nonzero, every element of the ideal class group of B is a q-th power.
a.notation: k = k̄, B Dedekind of finite type over k, q ∈ ℕ, q ≠ 0 in k ⇒ ∀ c ∈ Cl(B), ∃ d ∈ Cl(B), d^q = c
a.known_as: divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which is a quotient of the divisible group of points of the Jacobian of the projective completion
a.reference: David Mumford, Abelian Varieties, 1970
a.why: The published fact gives divisibility by every positive integer, multiples of the characteristic included, while the Lean statement allows only q prime to the characteristic, so it is weaker.

b.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field, B a Dedekind domain that is a finitely generated k-algebra, and q a natural number whose image in k is nonzero. Then every element of the ideal class group of B is a q-th power.
b.known_as: the divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which follows from the divisibility of the Jacobian and holds for every q ≥ 1

check.known_as: divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which is a quotient of the divisible group of points of the Jacobian of its smooth projective model
check.note: The published fact holds for every q ≥ 1, multiples of the characteristic included, while the Lean statement asks for q nonzero in k, and the trivial case B = k is allowed.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.Dict.ThetaHalf.exists_ne_zero_of_scaled
theorems.areas: complex analysis, inner product spaces, special functions, other analysis, topology, linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let V be a finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space with a bilinear form B, let p be an injective additive map from V to ℂ^g, and let L be a finitely generated subgroup of V whose image spans ℂ^g over ℝ and which equals its own dual for B/M, where M ≥ 2. Let H(z, w) = zᵀH w̄ be a positive definite Hermitian form with Im H(p(u), p(v)) = B(u, v), let c be a function of modulus one on V, and let f be a nonzero entire function on ℂ^g with f(z + p(v)) = c(v)·exp(πH(z, p(v)) + (π/2)H(p(v), p(v)))·f(z) for all v ∈ L. Then f(p(v)/M) ≠ 0 for some v ∈ L. Geometrically, f is a nonzero theta function for a polarization of type (M, …, M) on the abelian variety ℂ^g/p(L), and the claim is that it does not vanish at every M-torsion point.
a.notation: L = {x ∈ V | B(x, L) ⊂ Mℤ}, Im H(pu, pv) = B(u, v), f ≢ 0 entire, f(z + pv) = c(v)·e^{πH(z, pv) + (π/2)H(pv, pv)}·f(z) ∀ v ∈ L ⇒ ∃ v ∈ L, f(M⁻¹p(v)) ≠ 0
a.known_as: non-vanishing of a nonzero theta function of level M at some M-division point, which follows from Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of a line bundle, together with the base-point freeness of the M-th power of a principal polarization for M ≥ 2
a.reference: David Mumford, On the equations defining abelian varieties I, Inventiones Mathematicae 1, 1966
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by the M-th power of a Riemann theta function on a principally polarized torus, and the variable line about a CM field E and a number r does not enter the statement.
a.why: I checked that the claim follows from the theta-group argument, but I know no source that states it in this form, so the relation rests on that deduction.

b.states: Let V be a finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space with a ℚ-bilinear form B and an injective additive map p into ℂ^g. Let L be a finitely generated subgroup of V that equals its own dual for M⁻¹B, with M ≥ 2, and whose image spans ℂ^g over ℝ. Let H be a positive definite Hermitian matrix with Im H(p u, p v) = B(u, v), where H(z, w) = zᵀ H w̄, let c be a function on V of absolute value 1, and let f be a nonzero entire function on ℂ^g with f(z + p v) = c(v) exp(π H(z, p v) + (π/2) H(p v, p v)) f(z) for all v in L. Then f(M⁻¹ p v) ≠ 0 for some v in L, and the variables E and r of the variable line do not occur in the statement.
b.known_as: the nonvanishing of a nonzero theta function of type (N, …, N), N ≥ 2, at some N-division point, a consequence of the irreducibility of Mumford's theta-group (Heisenberg) representation and the base-point freeness of N times a principal polarization
b.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses force p(L) to be a lattice of rank 2g carrying a polarization of type (M, …, M), and a nonzero f exists whenever c is a semicharacter.

check.known_as: a corollary of Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of an ample line bundle, combined with the base-point freeness of line bundles of type (M, …, M) for M ≥ 2, by which a nonzero theta function of this type does not vanish at every M-torsion point
check.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses force p(L) to be a lattice of rank 2g with a polarization of type (M, …, M), and a nonzero f exists whenever c restricted to L is a semicharacter for B.
check.note: The variable line about a CM field E and a number r does not enter the statement, and no source I know states the claim in this form, so the relation rests on the deduction from the theta-group theorem.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.pic_divisible_dedekind_finiteType_algClosed
theorems.areas: ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field, B a Dedekind domain that is a finitely generated k-algebra, and q a natural number that is invertible in k. Then every element of the Picard group of B, the group of isomorphism classes of invertible B-modules, is a q-th power. For a Dedekind domain the Picard group is the ideal class group, so this is the claim of dossier 86 in another notation.
a.notation: k = k̄, B Dedekind of finite type over k, q ∈ k^× ⇒ ∀ c ∈ Pic(B), ∃ d ∈ Pic(B), d^q = c
a.known_as: divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which is a quotient of the divisible group of points of the Jacobian of the projective completion
a.reference: David Mumford, Abelian Varieties, 1970
a.why: The published fact gives divisibility by every positive integer, while the Lean statement allows only q invertible in k, so it is weaker.

b.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field, B a Dedekind domain that is a finitely generated k-algebra, and q a natural number that is a unit in k. Then every element of the Picard group CommRing.Pic B is a q-th power.
b.known_as: the divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which follows from the divisibility of the Jacobian and holds for every q ≥ 1

check.known_as: divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, which is a quotient of the divisible group of points of the Jacobian of its smooth projective model
check.note: Statement 88 is statement 86 with the group of invertible modules in place of the ideal class group, which are isomorphic for a Dedekind domain, and with q a unit in k, which in a field means q nonzero.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.thetaFunction_ne_zero_at_divisionPoint_selfDual
theorems.areas: complex analysis, inner product spaces, special functions, other analysis, topology, linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let V be a finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space with a bilinear form B, let p be an injective additive map from V to ℂ^g, and let L be a finitely generated subgroup of V whose image spans ℂ^g over ℝ and which equals its own dual for B. Let H(z, w) = zᵀH w̄ be a positive definite Hermitian form with Im H(p(u), p(v)) = B(u, v), let c be a function of modulus one on V, let N ≥ 2, and let f be a nonzero entire function with f(z + p(v)) = c(v)·exp(N(πH(z, p(v)) + (π/2)H(p(v), p(v))))·f(z) for all v ∈ L. Then f(p(v)/N) ≠ 0 for some v ∈ L. Geometrically, f is a nonzero section of a line bundle algebraically equivalent to the N-th power of a principal polarization on ℂ^g/p(L), and the claim is that it does not vanish at every N-torsion point.
a.notation: L = {x ∈ V | B(x, L) ⊂ ℤ}, Im H(pu, pv) = B(u, v), f ≢ 0 entire, f(z + pv) = c(v)·e^{N(πH(z, pv) + (π/2)H(pv, pv))}·f(z) ∀ v ∈ L ⇒ ∃ v ∈ L, f(N⁻¹p(v)) ≠ 0
a.known_as: non-vanishing of a nonzero theta function of level N at some N-division point, which follows from Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of a line bundle, together with the base-point freeness of the N-th power of a principal polarization for N ≥ 2
a.reference: David Mumford, On the equations defining abelian varieties I, Inventiones Mathematicae 1, 1966
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by the N-th power of a Riemann theta function on a principally polarized torus, and the conclusion does not follow at once.
a.why: I checked that the claim follows from the theta-group argument, but I know no source that states it in this form, so the relation rests on that deduction.

b.states: Let V be a finite-dimensional ℚ-vector space with a ℚ-bilinear form B and an injective additive map p into ℂ^g. Let L be a finitely generated subgroup that equals its own dual for B and whose image spans ℂ^g over ℝ, let H be a positive definite Hermitian matrix with Im H(p u, p v) = B(u, v), and let c be a function on V of absolute value 1. Take N ≥ 2 and a nonzero entire function f on ℂ^g with f(z + p v) = c(v) exp(N(π H(z, p v) + (π/2) H(p v, p v))) f(z) for all v in L. Then f(N⁻¹ p v) ≠ 0 for some v in L.
b.known_as: the nonvanishing of a nonzero theta function of type (N, …, N), N ≥ 2, at some N-division point, a consequence of the irreducibility of Mumford's theta-group (Heisenberg) representation and the base-point freeness of N times a principal polarization
b.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses describe a principally polarized lattice, and a nonzero f exists for a suitable c.

check.known_as: a corollary of Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of an ample line bundle, combined with the base-point freeness of line bundles of type (N, …, N) for N ≥ 2, by which a nonzero theta function of this type does not vanish at every N-torsion point
check.vacuity: None found, because L is unimodular for B, p(L) is then a lattice, and a nonzero f exists whenever c restricted to L is a semicharacter for N·B.
check.note: Here the factor c(v) stands outside the N-th power while the exponent is multiplied by N, so f is a theta function for the Hermitian form N·H, which has type (N, …, N).

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_place_not_isSquare_adicCompletion
theorems.areas: number fields, ring theory

a.states: Let F be a number field, u a nonzero element that is not a square in F, and S₀ a finite set of nonzero primes of the ring of integers. Then some nonzero prime v outside S₀ has u not a square in the completion F_v.
a.notation: u ∈ F^× ∖ F^{×2}, S₀ finite ⇒ ∃ finite place v ∉ S₀ with u ∉ F_v^{×2}
a.known_as: the case n = 2 of the Grunwald–Wang theorem in contrapositive form, which says that an element that is a square in all but finitely many completions is a square
a.reference: Emil Artin and John Tate, Class Field Theory, 1968, Chapter X
a.vacuity: The hypothesis u ≠ 0 is redundant because 0 is a square, and the hypotheses can be met, for example by F = ℚ and u = 2.
a.why: The statement is the contrapositive of the local–global principle for squares away from a finite set, which is a standard corollary of Chebotarev's theorem and the case n = 2 of Grunwald–Wang.

b.states: Let F be a number field, u a nonzero non-square in F and S₀ a finite set of finite places. Then at some finite place v outside S₀ the image of u is not a square in the completion F_v.
b.known_as: the local–global principle that an element of a number field which is a square in almost all completions is a square in the field, here in contrapositive form (the case n = 2 of the theorem on local n-th powers, proved with the Chebotarev density theorem)
b.vacuity: The hypothesis u ≠ 0 is redundant because 0 is a square, but no hypothesis is impossible to meet.

check.known_as: the case n = 2 of the Grunwald–Wang theorem on local powers in contrapositive form, which says that an element of a number field that is a square in all but finitely many completions is a square
check.vacuity: The hypothesis u ≠ 0 is redundant because 0 is a square, and the hypotheses can be met, for example by F = ℚ and u = 2.
check.note: Because S₀ is an arbitrary finite set, the conclusion gives infinitely many finite places at which u is not a square.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.ThetaDivisionPoints.exists_ne_zero_of_principal
theorems.areas: complex analysis, inner product spaces, special functions, other analysis, topology, linear algebra

a.states: Let Λ be a discrete subgroup of ℂ^g that spans ℂ^g over ℝ, H(z, w) = zᵀH w̄ a positive definite Hermitian form, χ a function of modulus one on Λ, and E an integer-valued bilinear form on Λ with E(l, m) = Im H(l, m) that induces a bijection from Λ onto Hom(Λ, ℤ). Let n ≥ 2 and let f be a nonzero entire function with f(z + l) = (χ(l)·exp(πH(z, l) + (π/2)H(l, l)))^n·f(z) for all l ∈ Λ. Then f(l/n) ≠ 0 for some l ∈ Λ. Geometrically, f is a nonzero section of the n-th power of a principal polarization on the torus ℂ^g/Λ, and the claim is that it does not vanish at every n-torsion point.
a.notation: Λ ⊂ ℂ^g lattice, Im H|_Λ unimodular, f ≢ 0 entire, f(z + l) = (χ(l)·e^{πH(z, l) + (π/2)H(l, l)})^n·f(z) ∀ l ∈ Λ ⇒ ∃ l ∈ Λ, f(l/n) ≠ 0
a.known_as: non-vanishing of a nonzero section of the n-th power of a principal polarization at some n-torsion point, which follows from Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of a line bundle, together with the base-point freeness of that power for n ≥ 2
a.reference: David Mumford, On the equations defining abelian varieties I, Inventiones Mathematicae 1, 1966
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by the n-th power of a Riemann theta function, and the conclusion does not follow at once.
a.why: I checked that the claim follows from the theta-group argument, but I know no source that states it in this form, so the relation rests on that deduction.

b.states: Let Λ be a discrete subgroup of ℂ^g that spans ℂ^g over ℝ, and let H be a positive definite Hermitian matrix whose imaginary part restricts to a unimodular integer-valued form on Λ. Let χ be a function on Λ of absolute value 1, take n ≥ 2, and let f be a nonzero entire function with f(z + l) = (χ(l) exp(π H(z, l) + (π/2) H(l, l)))^n f(z) for all l in Λ. Then f(n⁻¹ l) ≠ 0 for some l in Λ.
