b.known_as: the nonvanishing of a nonzero theta function of type (N, …, N), N ≥ 2, at some N-division point, a consequence of the irreducibility of Mumford's theta-group (Heisenberg) representation and the base-point freeness of N times a principal polarization
b.vacuity: None found, because a nonzero section of the n-th power of a principal polarization exists for a suitable χ.

check.known_as: a corollary of Mumford's theorem that the theta group acts irreducibly on the sections of an ample line bundle, combined with the base-point freeness of the n-th power of a principal polarization for n ≥ 2, by which a nonzero section of that power does not vanish at every n-torsion point
check.vacuity: None found, because a nonzero section of the n-th power of a principal polarization exists, for example the n-th power of a Riemann theta function with χ a semicharacter.
check.note: Statements 87, 89 and 91 make the same claim in three presentations, with the lattice given through V and p in the first two and directly as a discrete subgroup of ℂ^g in the third.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.CMData.exists_field
theorems.areas: number fields, algebraic geometry, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K be a quadratic number field and σ a non-real embedding of K into ℂ, so that K is imaginary quadratic. Then there is a number field M inside ℂ containing σ(K) such that every invertible fractional ideal I of 𝒪_K has a Weierstrass curve W over 𝒪_M with unit discriminant. For this W, every lattice L′ with c₄(W) = 12g₂(L′) and Δ(W) = g₂(L′)³ − 27g₃(L′)² is a nonzero complex multiple of σ(I). The equations c₄ = 12g₂ and Δ = g₂³ − 27g₃² hold for the model y² = x³ − (g₂/4)x − g₃/4 of ℂ/L′, so the claim says that W is a model of the elliptic curve ℂ/σ(I) with good reduction at every prime of M.
a.notation: K imaginary quadratic ⇒ ∃ number field M ⊃ σ(K), ∀ I ∈ I_K, ∃ W over 𝒪_M with Δ(W) ∈ 𝒪_M^×, ∀ L′ (c₄(W) = 12g₂(L′) ∧ Δ(W) = g₂(L′)³ − 27g₃(L′)² ⇒ L′ ∈ ℂ^×·σ(I))
a.known_as: everywhere good reduction of the elliptic curves with complex multiplication by 𝒪_K over one suitable number field, which rests on the Serre–Tate theorem that such curves have potentially good reduction at every prime
a.reference: Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties, Annals of Mathematics 88, 1968
a.why: The local content is Serre–Tate potential good reduction, but one field for all ideal classes and a global model with unit discriminant need further steps, so the statement claims more than the cited result.

b.states: Let K be an imaginary quadratic field with a non-real embedding σ into ℂ. Then there is a subfield M of ℂ of finite degree over ℚ that contains σ(K) and has the following property. For every invertible fractional ideal I of 𝓞_K there is a Weierstrass curve W over 𝓞_M with unit discriminant, and every period pair L' with c₄(W) = 12 g₂(L') and Δ(W) = g₂(L')³ − 27 g₃(L')² has lattice c·σ(I) for some nonzero complex c. The two equations force j(L') = j(W), so the claim amounts to W being a model of ℂ/σ(I) over 𝓞_M with good reduction everywhere.
b.known_as: the fact that an elliptic curve with complex multiplication, whose j-invariant is an algebraic integer, acquires good reduction everywhere over a suitable number field, with a global Weierstrass model of unit discriminant (potential good reduction everywhere, as in Serre–Tate, made global)
b.vacuity: None found, because the discriminant of W is a unit and hence nonzero, so period pairs that satisfy the two equations exist by the uniformization theorem.

check.known_as: potential good reduction everywhere of elliptic curves with complex multiplication (Serre and Tate), in the global form of a Weierstrass model with unit discriminant over one number field for all curves with complex multiplication by 𝒪_K
check.vacuity: None found, because a unit discriminant is nonzero in ℂ, so period pairs that meet the two equations exist and the inner claim has content.
check.note: The two equations on L′ fix g₂(L′) and fix g₃(L′) up to sign, so the conclusion says exactly that W has the j-invariant of σ(I), and the statement covers only curves with complex multiplication by the maximal order, which is narrower than the Serre–Tate theorem even though its conclusion asks for more.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.graded_bezout_bound
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K be algebraically closed and T an ℕ-graded K-algebra that is a domain of Krull dimension g + 1 with g ≥ 1, finite over the subalgebra generated by degree-one elements x₁, …, x_m, and with dim_K T_e ≤ (Ne)^g for all e ≥ 1. Let s be a nonzero element of degree d and F a set of elements of degree a, and assume that only finitely many K-points of Proj T vanish on F, where a K-point is a K-algebra map T → K that does not kill all x_i, taken up to the scaling φ(y) = c^e ψ(y) on T_e. Then any family of pairwise inequivalent K-points that vanish on s and on F has at most N^g · g! · d · a^{g−1} members.
a.notation: X = Proj T, dim X = g, dim T_e ≤ (Ne)^g, #(X ∩ V(F)) < ∞ ⇒ #(X ∩ V(F) ∩ V(s)) ≤ N^g · g! · d · a^{g−1}
a.known_as: a Bézout inequality for the points of a projective variety cut out by hypersurfaces, with the degree of the variety bounded by N^g g! through its Hilbert function
a.reference: William Fulton, Intersection Theory, 1984, Example 8.4.6
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by a polynomial ring in g + 1 variables with N = 2 and F = {x₁^a, …, x_g^a}, and the conclusion does not follow at once.
a.why: The bound is what refined Bézout gives after cutting X by g − 1 general members of the span of F and by s, but the exact packaging with the Hilbert-function bound is specific to one proof.

b.states: Let K be algebraically closed and T an ℕ-graded K-domain. Assume that T is finite over the subalgebra generated by degree-one elements x₁, …, x_m, has Krull dimension g + 1 with g ≥ 1, and satisfies dim 𝒜_e ≤ (Ne)^g for all e ≥ 1. Let s ≠ 0 be homogeneous of degree d, and let F be a set of degree-a elements with finitely many common projective zeros, where a projective point is a K-algebra map T → K that is nonzero on some x_i, taken up to scaling by c^e in degree e. Then n pairwise non-proportional projective points at which s and every element of F vanish satisfy n ≤ N^g · g! · d · a^(g−1).
b.known_as: a Bézout inequality for a projective variety X of dimension g, which bounds the isolated points of X cut by a hypersurface of degree d and hypersurfaces of degree a by deg X · d · a^(g−1), with deg X ≤ g! N^g read off the Hilbert function (refined Bézout theorem, Fulton, Intersection Theory, Chapter 8)
b.vacuity: The finiteness hypothesis cannot hold when F is empty, since a projective variety of positive dimension has infinitely many points, but suitable nonempty F meet it.

check.known_as: a Bézout inequality for a projective variety X of dimension g whose degree is at most g!·N^g by its Hilbert function, bounding the points cut out by a form of degree d and forms of degree a with finitely many common zeros by deg X · d · a^(g−1), a consequence of the refined Bézout theorem (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Example 8.4.6)
check.vacuity: None found, because the polynomial ring in g + 1 variables with N = 2 and F = {x₁^a, …, x_g^a} meets the hypotheses, while an empty F would make the finiteness hypothesis fail.
check.note: The exponent g − 1 on a, in place of g, comes from cutting X first by s and then by g − 1 general combinations of F, and the finiteness of the common zeros of F is what keeps each cut proper.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.IdCompOpen.isOpen_sectionComponents_of_family
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, topology, homological algebra, combinatorics, geometry

a.states: Let f be a smooth morphism of schemes from X to S with a section e, and let C be the set of points x of X that lie in the connected component of the fibre f⁻¹(f(x)) containing e(f(x)). Suppose O assigns to each open set U of X an open set O(U), such that every y ∈ C with e(f(y)) ∈ U lies in O(U), and such that every y ∈ O(U) lies in C whenever all points of U in the fibre of y lie in C. Then C is open in X.
a.notation: f ∈ Hom(X, S) smooth, f ∘ e = id_S, C = {x ∈ X | x ∈ connected component of f⁻¹(f(x)) through e(f(x))}, (h1), (h2) ⇒ C open in X
a.known_as: openness of the union of the connected components of the fibres that meet a section of a smooth morphism, which is the identity component in the case of group schemes, here with two extra hypotheses on an auxiliary family of open sets
a.reference: Alexander Grothendieck and Jean Dieudonné, Éléments de géométrie algébrique IV, troisième partie, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 28, 1966, §15.6
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met by the constant family O(U) = C, which is open by the published theorem, and they do not give the conclusion without smoothness, since for Spec R[t]/(t(t − π)) over a discrete valuation ring with the section t = 0 suitable O exist while C is not open.
a.why: The conclusion is the EGA openness statement, and the two auxiliary hypotheses reduce it to finding an open neighbourhood of the section inside C, which is the step that uses smoothness.

b.states: Let f from X to S be a smooth morphism of schemes with a section e, and let O assign an open set O(U) to each open U of X. The first condition on O is that a point y lying in the connected component of its fibre through e(f(y)) belongs to O(U) whenever e(f(y)) lies in U. The second condition is that a point y of O(U) lies in that connected component whenever every point of U in the fibre of y does. Then the set of points x that lie in the connected component of the fibre f⁻¹(f(x)) containing e(f(x)) is open in X.
b.known_as: the openness of the union of the connected components of the fibres that meet the section, for a smooth morphism with a section (for instance EGA IV 15.6.5, and SGA 3 VI_B 3.10 for the identity component of a smooth group scheme)
b.vacuity: None found, because the published theorem makes the target set open, so taking O(U) equal to that set meets both conditions, which are therefore superfluous rather than impossible.

check.known_as: openness of the union of the connected components of the fibres that meet a section of a smooth morphism (EGA IV 15.6.5, and SGA 3 VI_B 3.10 for the identity component of a smooth group scheme)
check.vacuity: None found, because the constant family O(U) = C meets the two conditions once C is known to be open, and the conditions do not give openness without smoothness, as the scheme Spec R[t]/(t(t − π)) over a discrete valuation ring with the section t = 0 shows.
check.note: The two conditions on O reduce openness of C to the existence, at each point of the section, of an open neighbourhood that lies inside C, and that step is where smoothness enters.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.ZetaDoubling.dblA
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: For a lattice L in ℂ and a point z with z ∉ L and 2z ∉ L, the Weierstrass function satisfies ℘(2z) = ℘(z) − (12℘(z)℘′(z)² − (6℘(z)² − g₂/2)²)/(4℘′(z)²). The identity ℘″ = 6℘² − g₂/2 turns the right side into (℘″(z)/℘′(z))²/4 − 2℘(z).
a.known_as: duplication formula for the Weierstrass ℘-function
a.reference: E. T. Whittaker and G. N. Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, fourth edition, 1927, Chapter XX
a.why: The formula is the classical duplication formula after the substitution ℘″ = 6℘² − g₂/2, and the hypothesis 2z ∉ L is exactly the condition ℘′(z) ≠ 0.

b.states: For every period pair L and every z with z and 2z outside the lattice, ℘(2z) = ℘(z) − (12℘(z)℘'(z)² − (6℘(z)² − g₂/2)²)/℘'(z)²/4. This rearranges to ℘(2z) = (6℘(z)² − g₂/2)²/(4℘'(z)²) − 2℘(z).
b.known_as: the duplication formula for the Weierstrass ℘-function, ℘(2z) = ¼(℘''(z)/℘'(z))² − 2℘(z) with ℘'' = 6℘² − g₂/2
b.vacuity: None found, since 2z outside the lattice makes ℘'(z) nonzero, so the division is genuine.

check.known_as: duplication formula for the Weierstrass ℘-function
check.note: The right side equals (℘″(z)/℘′(z))²/4 − 2℘(z) through ℘″ = 6℘² − g₂/2, and the hypothesis 2z ∉ L is exactly what makes ℘′(z) nonzero for z ∉ L.

theorems.name: UpperTheory.Kd.K4.cdAbs
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, field theory, group theory

a.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and K a finite extension of k(X) with the induced k[X]-structure, let m, m′ > 0, and let f ∈ K be nonzero such that at every valuation ring B of K containing k[X], f equals a unit of B times an m-th power. Then there is a nonzero h ∈ K such that at every such B, f/h^m equals a unit times an (mm′)-th power. In terms of divisors on the affine curve C over the X-line, if div(f) = mD, then the class of D in Cl(C) is divisible by m′.
a.notation: div_C(f) = mD ⇒ ∃ h ∈ K^×, div_C(f/h^m) ∈ mm′·Div(C), equivalently [D] ∈ m′·Cl(C)
a.known_as: a consequence of the divisibility of the divisor class group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, applied to divisor classes that are m-torsion
a.reference: David Mumford, Abelian Varieties, 1970
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by f = 1, and the conclusion does not follow at once.
a.why: The translation into divisor classes is direct, and the statement needs divisibility only for m-torsion classes in a valuation-ring form, which makes it weaker and shaped for one use.

b.states: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and K a finite extension of k(X) that is compatible with k[X]. Take m > 0 and m' > 0, and let f be a nonzero element of K that equals a unit times an m-th power at every valuation subring of K containing k[X]. Then there is a nonzero h in K such that f/h^m equals a unit times an (m·m')-th power at every such valuation subring.
b.known_as: the divisibility of the Picard group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, applied to the divisor class (1/m)·div(f) to divide it by m'

check.known_as: a consequence of the divisibility of the divisor class group of a smooth affine curve over an algebraically closed field, applied to the m-torsion class of div(f)/m
check.note: In terms of divisors on the affine curve C over the X-line, the statement says that if div(f) = mD, then the class of D in Cl(C) is divisible by m′.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.JR.UnramInt.alg_main
theorems.areas: other analysis, topology, linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let F be a non-archimedean local field, given as a complete, locally compact, ultrametric nontrivially normed field, and let E be a finite normed extension of F with the same value group, so that E/F is unramified. Let K be a finite extension of F and L a quadratic extension of K generated over K by the image of E, with all maps compatible. Then there are ϖ ∈ K^× and the ring O of elements of L with spectral norm at most 1 such that ϖ is not a norm from L, ϖ generates the maximal ideal of O, the trace maps O onto 𝒪_K, every unit of 𝒪_K is the norm of an element of O, multiplication by powers of ϖ shrinks O uniformly to zero, and every element of L becomes integral after multiplication by some power of ϖ.
a.notation: dim_K L = 2, L = K·E, e(E/F) = 1 ⇒ ∃ ϖ ∈ K^×, O = {y ∈ L | ‖y‖ ≤ 1}, ϖ ∉ N_{L/K}(L), 𝔪_O = ϖO, Tr_{L/K}(O) = 𝒪_K, 𝒪_K^× ⊂ N_{L/K}(O), sup_{z ∈ O} ‖ϖ^n z‖ → 0, L = ⋃_n ϖ^{−n}O
a.known_as: standard properties of an unramified quadratic extension of local fields, namely that a uniformizer of the base stays a uniformizer and is not a norm, while units are norms and the trace on integers is surjective
a.reference: Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields, 1979, Chapters III and V
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example by F = K = ℚ_p and E = L the unramified quadratic extension of ℚ_p, and the conclusion does not follow at once.
a.why: Each clause is a textbook fact about unramified extensions, but the bundle for a quadratic extension presented as a compositum with E is shaped for one construction.

b.states: Let F be a non-archimedean local field, E a finite extension of F with the same value group (hence unramified), K a finite extension of F, and L a quadratic extension of K generated over K by the image of E. Then there are an element ϖ of K^× and the subring O of L of elements of spectral norm at most 1 with these properties. The element ϖ is not a norm from L, it lies in O as a non-unit, and every element of O is a multiple of ϖ in O or a unit of O. Moreover, the trace maps O onto the integers of K, every unit among the integers of K is the norm of an element of O, the sets ϖ^n O shrink to 0 in spectral norm, and every element of L lies in O after multiplication by some power of ϖ.
b.known_as: the standard properties of an unramified extension of local fields, here of degree 2 (the valuation ring is the closed unit ball, a uniformiser of K stays a uniformiser and is not a norm, the trace is surjective on integers and the norm is surjective on units, as in Serre, Local Fields, Chapter V)

a_errors: A writes that the trace maps O onto 𝒪_K, while the Lean text states only that every s of K lying in O is the trace of some z in O and leaves the inclusion of the traces of O in 𝒪_K unstated.
b_errors: B writes that the trace maps O onto the integers of K, while the Lean text states only that every s of K lying in O is the trace of some z in O and leaves the inclusion of the traces of O in the integers of K unstated.
check.known_as: the standard properties of an unramified quadratic extension of non-archimedean local fields, by which a uniformizer of the base stays a uniformizer and is not a norm, every unit is the norm of an integer and the trace on integers is surjective (Serre, Local Fields, Chapters III and V)
check.vacuity: None found, because F = K = ℚ_p with E = L the unramified quadratic extension of ℚ_p meets the hypotheses.
check.note: The extension L/K is unramified because E has the value group of F and generates L over K, and every clause of the conclusion rests on that property, which the statement never names.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.OriginCoordinatesAdd.stepA
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: For a lattice L in ℂ and points z and w with z, w, z − w and z + w outside L, ℘(z + w) = ℘(z) − ((6℘(z)² − g₂/2)(℘(z) − ℘(w)) − (℘′(z) − ℘′(w))℘′(z))/(2(℘(z) − ℘(w))²). The differential equation ℘′² = 4℘³ − g₂℘ − g₃ shows that the right side equals (1/4)((℘′(z) − ℘′(w))/(℘(z) − ℘(w)))² − ℘(z) − ℘(w), so the statement is the addition theorem in a rearranged form.
a.known_as: addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function, written in a rearranged algebraic form
a.reference: E. T. Whittaker and G. N. Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, fourth edition, 1927, Chapter XX
a.why: I checked that the identity is equivalent to the classical addition formula through the Weierstrass differential equation, and its unusual shape points to an intermediate step of a proof.

b.states: For every period pair L and all z and w such that z, w, z − w and z + w lie outside the lattice, ℘(z + w) = ℘(z) − ((6℘(z)² − g₂/2)(℘(z) − ℘(w)) − (℘'(z) − ℘'(w))℘'(z))/(℘(z) − ℘(w))²/2.
b.known_as: the addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function, rewritten with the differential equation ℘'² = 4℘³ − g₂℘ − g₃ into a form whose limit as w tends to z gives the duplication formula
b.vacuity: None found, since z ± w outside the lattice makes ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w).

check.known_as: addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function, rewritten with the differential equation ℘′² = 4℘³ − g₂℘ − g₃ into a form whose limit as w tends to z can be taken
check.note: The hypotheses z − w ∉ L and z + w ∉ L together make ℘(z) − ℘(w) nonzero, which is what the division needs.

theorems.name: Formalism.L2.Th1.E.AddThm.collinear
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: For a lattice L and points z and w with z, w and z + w outside L, (℘(z) − ℘(w))℘′(z + w) = −((℘′(z) − ℘′(w))(℘(z + w) − ℘(z)) + ℘′(z)(℘(z) − ℘(w))). The identity says that the points (℘(z), ℘′(z)), (℘(w), ℘′(w)) and (℘(z + w), −℘′(z + w)) of the curve y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃ lie on one line.
a.known_as: the determinant form of the addition theorem for ℘, which says that the points (℘(u), ℘′(u)), (℘(v), ℘′(v)) and (℘(w), ℘′(w)) are collinear when u + v + w = 0
a.reference: E. T. Whittaker and G. N. Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, fourth edition, 1927, Chapter XX
a.vacuity: Both sides vanish when z − w lies in L, but for other z and w the identity has content and the hypotheses can be met.
a.why: Expanding the vanishing three-by-three determinant for the points at z, w and −(z + w), with ℘′ odd, gives exactly this identity.

b.states: For every period pair L and all z and w such that z, w and z + w lie outside the lattice, (℘(z) − ℘(w))℘'(z + w) = −((℘'(z) − ℘'(w))(℘(z + w) − ℘(z)) + ℘'(z)(℘(z) − ℘(w))). The identity says that the points (℘(z), ℘'(z)), (℘(w), ℘'(w)) and (℘(z + w), −℘'(z + w)) lie on one line.
b.known_as: the collinearity form of the addition theorem, by which the points of the Weierstrass cubic with parameters u, v and w satisfying u + v + w ≡ 0 lie on one line (the vanishing of the determinant with rows 1, ℘, ℘', Whittaker and Watson, Chapter 20)
b.vacuity: None found, and when z − w lies in the lattice both sides vanish, so the statement needs no hypothesis on z − w.

check.known_as: the collinearity or determinant form of the addition theorem for ℘, by which the points of y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃ with parameters u, v and w satisfying u + v + w ≡ 0 lie on one line (Whittaker and Watson, §20.3)
check.vacuity: None found, although both sides vanish when z − w lies in L, so the identity has content only when z − w lies outside L.
check.note: The identity is written with the denominator ℘(z) − ℘(w) cleared, which is why it needs no hypothesis on z − w.

theorems.name: Formalism.L2.Th1.E.AddThm.P_add
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: For a lattice L and points z and w with z, w, z + w and z − w outside L, ℘(z + w) = (1/4)((℘′(z) − ℘′(w))/(℘(z) − ℘(w)))² − ℘(z) − ℘(w).
a.known_as: addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function
a.reference: E. T. Whittaker and G. N. Watson, A Course of Modern Analysis, fourth edition, 1927, Chapter XX
a.why: The formula and its hypotheses match the classical addition theorem, since z ± w ∉ L is exactly the condition ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w) and z + w ∉ L keeps the left side finite.

b.states: For every period pair L and all z and w such that z, w, z + w and z − w lie outside the lattice, ℘(z + w) = ¼((℘'(z) − ℘'(w))/(℘(z) − ℘(w)))² − ℘(z) − ℘(w).
b.known_as: the addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function
b.vacuity: None found, since z ± w outside the lattice makes the denominator ℘(z) − ℘(w) nonzero.

check.known_as: addition theorem for the Weierstrass ℘-function
check.note: For z and w outside L the hypothesis z ± w ∉ L is equivalent to ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w), so the four hypotheses are exactly the classical ones.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.pNeg
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Let L be the lattice of a period pair in ℂ, and let ℘ and ℘′ be its Weierstrass function and the derivative of that function. Take complex numbers z and w that lie outside L with ℘(z) = ℘(w) and ℘′(z) = −℘′(w). Then z + w lies in L.
a.known_as: injectivity of the Weierstrass parametrization z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) on ℂ/L without the origin, applied to z and −w, using that ℘ is even and ℘′ is odd
a.reference: Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 1986, Chapter VI
a.why: The hypotheses say that z and −w have the same image under the parametrization, so the statement is the injectivity part of the textbook isomorphism between ℂ/L and the complex points of y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃.

b.states: Let L be a period pair and let z and w be complex numbers outside its lattice. If ℘(z) = ℘(w) and ℘′(z) = −℘′(w), then z + w lies in the lattice. Put differently, two points of (ℂ/L)∖{0} that the map z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) sends to opposite points of the Weierstrass curve are themselves opposite in ℂ/L.
b.known_as: Injectivity of the Weierstrass parametrization z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) on (ℂ/L)∖{0}, applied to z and −w, which is part of the uniformization ℂ/L ≅ E(ℂ) (Silverman, AEC Prop. VI.3.6)

check.known_as: Injectivity of the Weierstrass parametrization z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) on (ℂ/L) ∖ {0}, part of the uniformization ℂ/L ≅ E(ℂ) (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Proposition VI.3.6), applied to z and −w
check.note: Because ℘ is even and ℘′ is odd, the hypotheses say that z and −w have the same image under (℘, ℘′), so the statement is theorem 103 applied to z and −w.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.weierstrassP_superlattice_half_period_prod
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Let L ⊆ L′ be period lattices in ℂ. Let T be a finite set of points of L′ outside L that are pairwise incongruent modulo L and that, together with 0, represent every class of L′/L. Let w be a point with 2w ∈ L and w ∉ L′. Then for every z ∉ L′, the product of ℘_{L′}(z) − ℘_{L′}(w) with the factors ℘_L(z) − ℘_L(t) for t ∈ T equals the product of ℘_L(z) − ℘_L(w) with the factors ℘_L(z) − ℘_L(w + t) for t ∈ T.
a.known_as: no published result known, an identity of elliptic functions that writes ℘_{L′} − ℘_{L′}(w) as a rational function of ℘_L for the isogeny ℂ/L → ℂ/L′, of the kind behind Vélu's isogeny formulas
a.vacuity: No hypothesis is impossible, and the identity is trivial only in the degenerate case L′ = L with T empty.
a.why: I checked that both sides are L-elliptic functions with the same divisor and the same leading term at 0, but I know this exact identity only as a computation inside isogeny arguments and not as a stated theorem.

b.states: Let L and L′ be period pairs with lattice of L contained in lattice of L′. Let T be a finite set of elements of L′ outside L that are pairwise incongruent modulo L and meet every class of L′ outside L, so T represents the nonzero classes of L′/L. Let w satisfy 2w ∈ L and w ∉ L′. Then for every z outside L′ the identity (℘_{L′}(z) − ℘_{L′}(w)) · ∏_{t∈T} (℘_L(z) − ℘_L(t)) = (℘_L(z) − ℘_L(w)) · ∏_{t∈T} (℘_L(z) − ℘_L(w + t)) holds.
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: No published result known, an identity of elliptic functions that writes ℘_{L′}(z) − ℘_{L′}(w) for a superlattice L′ ⊇ L and a half-period w of L outside L′ as a rational function of ℘_L(z), in the spirit of Vélu's isogeny formulas
check.vacuity: No hypothesis is impossible, and the identity holds at once only in the subcase L′ = L, where T is empty and both sides coincide.
check.note: Both sides are L-elliptic functions of z whose only pole is at 0, of order 2(|T| + 1) with leading coefficient 1, and whose zeros are double zeros at the points w + s for s in L′/L, so the identity can be checked by comparing divisors and leading terms.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.pInj
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Let L be the lattice of a period pair in ℂ. Take complex numbers z and w that lie outside L with ℘(z) = ℘(w) and ℘′(z) = ℘′(w), where ℘ is the Weierstrass function of L. Then z − w lies in L.
a.known_as: injectivity of the Weierstrass parametrization z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) on ℂ/L without the origin, part of the isomorphism of ℂ/L with the complex points of the elliptic curve y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃
a.reference: Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 1986, Chapter VI
a.why: The textbook theorem says that the parametrization is a bijection onto the affine points of the curve, and the Lean statement keeps only its injectivity.

b.states: Let L be a period pair and let z and w be complex numbers outside its lattice. If ℘(z) = ℘(w) and ℘′(z) = ℘′(w), then z − w lies in the lattice. So the map z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) is injective on (ℂ/L)∖{0}.
b.known_as: Injectivity part of the Weierstrass uniformization ℂ/L ≅ E(ℂ), z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) (Silverman, AEC Prop. VI.3.6)

check.known_as: Injectivity part of the Weierstrass uniformization ℂ/L ≅ E(ℂ), z ↦ (℘(z), ℘′(z)) (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Proposition VI.3.6)
check.note: The statement keeps only injectivity, while the textbook result also gives surjectivity onto the affine points of y² = 4x³ − g₂x − g₃ and compatibility with the group laws.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_continuous_normCharLFunction_ne_zero_one
theorems.areas: number fields, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, topology, ring theory

a.states: Let K be a number field, m a prime number and χ a character of (ℤ/mℤ)ˣ. Let cl be a map from the nonzero primes P of the ring of integers of K to (ℤ/mℤ)ˣ that sends every P whose norm N(P) is prime to m to the class of N(P). If χ(cl P) ≠ 1 for some P with m ∤ N(P), then there is a continuous function L on ℂ with L(1) ≠ 0. For every real s > 1 this L agrees with the exponential of the sum over P of −log(1 − χ(cl P) N(P)^{−s}), which is the Euler product ∏_P (1 − χ(cl P) N(P)^{−s})^{−1}.
a.known_as: nonvanishing at s = 1 of the L-function of a nontrivial finite-order Hecke character, here P ↦ χ(N(P) mod m), with Euler factors at the primes above m that use arbitrary roots of unity
a.reference: Jürgen Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, 1999, Chapter VII
a.why: The content follows from the classical nonvanishing of L(1, χ) for ray class characters. The Lean form keeps only a nonzero limit along real s → 1 and allows arbitrary factors at the primes above m, so both the relation and the kind are judgment calls.

b.states: Let K be a number field, m a prime, χ a character of (ℤ/m)ˣ, and cl a map from the nonzero primes P of 𝓞_K to (ℤ/m)ˣ that sends every P with m ∤ N(P) to N(P) mod m. Suppose χ(cl P) ≠ 1 for some P with m ∤ N(P). Then there is a continuous function L from ℂ to ℂ with L(1) ≠ 0 that equals exp(∑_P −log(1 − χ(cl P) N(P)^{−s})), which is the Euler product ∏_P (1 − χ(cl P) N(P)^{−s})^{−1}, at every real s > 1. L only has to agree with the Euler product for real s > 1, so the conclusion says that this product has a nonzero limit as s decreases to 1.
b.known_as: Non-vanishing at s = 1 of the L-function of a nontrivial ray class character (Hecke, Landau), here for the character χ ∘ N_{K/ℚ} with arbitrary unimodular Euler factors at the primes above m

check.known_as: Nonvanishing at s = 1 of the L-function of a nontrivial ray class character (Hecke, Landau), here for the character P ↦ χ(N(P) mod m), with arbitrary values of χ in the Euler factors at the primes above m
check.note: The function L has to agree with the Euler product only at real s > 1, so the conclusion says only that this product has a nonzero limit as s decreases to 1, and the statement covers only characters of the form χ ∘ N with m prime.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.KeyFourth.exists_eq_smul_pow
theorems.areas: complex analysis, other analysis, topology, linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let K be a field with a ring map to ℂ, and let A be a smooth K-algebra such that ℂ ⊗_K A is a domain. Let n > 0, let u be a unit of A and let C be a nonzero complex number. Suppose that ρ is a function on the K-algebra maps ψ from A to ℂ, that ρ is continuous along every holomorphic family of such maps over an open subset of some ℂ^m, and that ρ(ψ)^n = C ψ(u) for every ψ. Then u = a b^n for some nonzero a in K and some b in A.
a.notation: (ρ continuous on Hom_K(A, ℂ) ∧ ∀ ψ, ρ(ψ)^n = C ψ(u)) ⇒ ∃ a ∈ K^×, ∃ b ∈ A, u = a b^n
a.known_as: no published result known, a Kummer-type descent lemma saying that a unit on a smooth geometrically integral variety is an n-th power up to a constant once a constant multiple of it has a continuous n-th root on the complex points
a.why: The statement follows from the Riemann existence theorem, the structure of units modulo constants and Hilbert's Theorem 90, but I know no source that states it in this form.

b.states: Let K be a field embedded in ℂ and A a smooth K-algebra with ℂ ⊗_K A a domain. Let n > 0, let u be a unit of A, C a nonzero complex number, and ρ a complex function on the K-algebra maps A → ℂ that is continuous along every holomorphic family of such maps parametrized by an open subset of some ℂ^m. If ρ(ψ)^n = C · ψ(u) for every ψ, then u = a · b^n for some nonzero a ∈ K and some b ∈ A. In geometric terms, a unit of a smooth geometrically integral affine variety is a constant times an n-th power when C·u has a continuous n-th root on the complex points.
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: No published result known, a Kummer-type descent lemma saying that a unit on a smooth geometrically integral affine variety is a constant times an n-th power once a constant multiple of it has a continuous n-th root on the complex points
check.note: Continuity along holomorphic families amounts to continuity on the complex points in the analytic topology, because the complex points of the smooth variety form a complex manifold with holomorphic charts.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.ZeroDensityMult.zero_density_mult
theorems.areas: zeta and L-series, Dirichlet and multiplicative characters, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis

a.states: There is a constant C > 0 with the following property for every real Q ≥ 3. Take any finite set T of triples (q, χ, ρ) in which χ is a primitive Dirichlet character of modulus q ≤ Q and ρ is a zero of L(s, χ) with Re ρ ≥ 1 − 1/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. Then the orders of these zeros add up to at most C Q^{1/4}.
a.known_as: large sieve zero-density estimate for the family of primitive Dirichlet L-functions, in a weak instance close to the line Re s = 1
a.reference: Hugh L. Montgomery, Topics in Multiplicative Number Theory, 1971
a.why: Montgomery's estimate bounds the count in this region by Q^{0.023} times a power of log Q, far below Q^{1/4}, and the specific constants 1/400 and 1/4 mark the statement as an input to one later argument.

b.states: There is a constant C > 0 with the following property for every Q ≥ 3. Take any finite set T of triples (q, χ, ρ) in which χ is a primitive Dirichlet character of modulus q ≤ Q and ρ is a zero of L(s, χ) with Re ρ ≥ 1 − 1/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. The orders of these zeros then sum to at most C · Q^{1/4}. So the primitive Dirichlet L-functions of conductor at most Q have O(Q^{1/4}) zeros, counted with multiplicity, in the box Re s ≥ 1 − 1/400, |Im s| ≤ Q.
b.known_as: Zero-density estimate for the family of Dirichlet L-functions near Re s = 1, of the form ∑_{q≤Q} ∑*_χ N(σ, T, χ) ≪ (Q²T)^{c(1−σ)} log^B(QT) (large-sieve density theorems of Montgomery, Gallagher and Huxley)

check.known_as: Large sieve zero-density estimate for the family of primitive Dirichlet L-functions near Re s = 1 (Montgomery, Topics in Multiplicative Number Theory, 1971), in a weak instance
check.note: Density estimates of Montgomery's type bound this count by about Q^{9/401} times a power of log Q, so the exponent 1/4 leaves much room, and the trivial character of modulus 1 counts as primitive, which brings the zeros of the Riemann zeta function into the sum.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.ZetaDoubling.derivWeierstrassP_ne_zero
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Let L be the lattice of a period pair in ℂ, and let z be a point with z ∉ L and 2z ∉ L. Then the derivative ℘′(z) of the Weierstrass function of L is nonzero.
a.known_as: the zeros of ℘′ are exactly the three half periods modulo L
a.reference: Lars V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 1979, Chapter 7
a.vacuity: No hypothesis is impossible, but the hypothesis z ∉ L is redundant because it follows from 2z ∉ L.
a.why: The Lean statement is one direction of the textbook description of the zeros of ℘′.

b.states: Let L be a period pair and z a complex number with z ∉ L and 2z ∉ L. Then ℘′(z) is nonzero. So ℘′ vanishes only at half-periods. The hypothesis z ∉ L already follows from 2z ∉ L.
b.known_as: The zeros of ℘′ modulo the lattice are exactly the three nonzero half-periods (the direction that every zero is a half-period)

check.known_as: The zeros of ℘′ modulo L are exactly the three nonzero half-periods (the direction that ℘′ vanishes only at half-periods)
check.note: The hypothesis z ∉ L is redundant, because z ∈ L would give 2z ∈ L.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.rational_units_haar_character_one
theorems.areas: number fields, measure theory, topology

a.states: Let F be a number field, and assume as instances that its adele ring 𝔸_F is locally compact and that 2 is invertible in 𝔸_F. Then every nonzero a in F, viewed as a unit of 𝔸_F, has Haar character 1. This means that multiplication by a preserves Haar measure on 𝔸_F.
a.notation: ∀ a ∈ F^×, |a|_{𝔸_F} = μ(aE)/μ(E) = ∏_v |a|_v = 1 for a Haar measure μ on 𝔸_F
a.known_as: the product formula for a number field in Weil's adelic form, which says that the module of a principal idele is 1
a.reference: André Weil, Basic Number Theory, 1967
a.vacuity: No emptiness was found, since the adele ring is locally compact and 2 is invertible in it, so the two instance hypotheses always hold.
a.why: The Haar character of a unit acting on a locally compact ring is its module, and the triviality of the module on F^× is the adelic product formula.

b.states: Let F be a number field, with instance hypotheses that the adele ring 𝔸_F is locally compact and that 2 is invertible in it. Then every a ∈ Fˣ, viewed as an idele, has distributive Haar character 1. So multiplication by a principal idele preserves Haar measure on 𝔸_F, which means its idelic norm ∏_v |a|_v equals 1.
b.known_as: Product formula of Artin and Whaples (∏_v |a|_v = 1 for a ∈ Fˣ), in the form that the module of a principal idele acting on the adeles is 1

check.known_as: Product formula ∏_v |a|_v = 1 for a ∈ Fˣ (Artin and Whaples), in Weil's form that the module of a principal idele acting on the adele ring is 1 (Weil, Basic Number Theory)
check.note: The instance hypotheses that the adele ring is locally compact and that 2 is invertible in it hold for every number field, so they restrict nothing.

theorems.name: GroundTheory.Automorphic.exists_dixmierMalliavin_line
theorems.areas: measure theory, complex analysis, inner product spaces, other analysis, topology

a.states: Take any real sequence (M_p) and any ε > 0. Then there are a real sequence (c_p) for which ∑ |c_p| M_p converges and smooth complex functions g and h supported in [−ε, ε] with the following property. Every smooth F from ℝ to ℂ whose p-th derivative has absolute value at most M_p on [−ε, ε] for every p satisfies F(0) = ∑_p c_p ∫ F^{(p)} g + ∫ F h.
a.known_as: the one-dimensional lemma of Dixmier and Malliavin, δ = h + ∑ c_p (−1)^p g^{(p)} with ∑ |c_p| r_p < ∞, which drives their factorization theorem
a.reference: Jacques Dixmier and Paul Malliavin, Factorisations de fonctions et de vecteurs indéfiniment différentiables, 1978
a.vacuity: If some M_p is negative, no F meets the bounds and the claim holds trivially with c, g and h equal to zero, but for nonnegative sequences the statement has its full content.
a.why: After integration by parts the Lean statement is the Dixmier–Malliavin lemma, but it is tested only on functions with the given derivative bounds and I recall the original wording only roughly.

b.states: For every sequence M of real numbers and every ε > 0 there are real numbers c_p and smooth complex functions g and h on ℝ with supports in [−ε, ε] such that ∑_p |c_p| M_p converges. Moreover, every smooth complex function F on ℝ with |F^{(p)}(t)| ≤ M_p for all p and all t in [−ε, ε] satisfies F(0) = ∑_p c_p ∫ F^{(p)} g + ∫ F h. After integration by parts this writes the Dirac measure at 0 as ∑_p (−1)^p c_p g^{(p)} + h on that class of functions.
b.known_as: Dixmier–Malliavin lemma (Dixmier and Malliavin 1978), the one-variable decomposition of the Dirac measure that underlies their factorization theorem for smooth vectors
b.vacuity: If some M_p is negative, no F meets the bounds and the statement holds at once with c = 0, but for positive M it has real content.

check.known_as: Dixmier–Malliavin lemma (Dixmier and Malliavin, 1978), the one-variable decomposition δ = h + ∑_p (−1)^p c_p g^{(p)} that underlies their factorization theorem
check.vacuity: Only in the subcase where some M_p is negative does the conclusion hold at once, since no F meets the bounds and c, g and h equal to zero work, while for nonnegative M the statement has its full content.
check.note: The identity is required only for smooth F whose derivatives obey the bounds M_p on [−ε, ε], and integration by parts turns it into the usual distributional form of the lemma.

theorems.name: Formalism.L2.Th1.E.AddThm.P_sub_ne
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Fix the lattice L of a period pair in ℂ as a variable. Take points z and w such that z, w, z + w and z − w all lie outside L. Then ℘(z) − ℘(w) ≠ 0, where ℘ is the Weierstrass function of L.
a.known_as: the fact that ℘(z) = ℘(w) holds exactly when z ≡ ±w modulo L
a.reference: Lars V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 1979, Chapter 7
a.why: The Lean statement is the nontrivial direction of the textbook fact that ℘ takes a given value only at a pair ±w modulo L.

b.states: Let L be a period pair and let z and w be complex numbers such that z, w, z + w and z − w all lie outside the lattice. Then ℘(z) − ℘(w) is nonzero.
b.known_as: ℘(z) = ℘(w) if and only if z ≡ ±w modulo the lattice (the direction that z ≢ ±w forces ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w))

check.known_as: ℘(z) = ℘(w) holds exactly when z ≡ ±w modulo L (the direction that z ≢ ±w forces ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w))
check.note: Theorem 111 states the same with the hypotheses z + w ∉ L and z − w ∉ L in the other order.

theorems.name: PI.GalTorsConj.W.OriginCoordinatesAdd.wp_ne
theorems.areas: special functions

a.states: Let L be the lattice of a period pair in ℂ, and take points z and w such that z, w, z − w and z + w all lie outside L. Then ℘(z) − ℘(w) ≠ 0, where ℘ is the Weierstrass function of L.
a.known_as: the fact that ℘(z) = ℘(w) holds exactly when z ≡ ±w modulo L
a.reference: Lars V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 1979, Chapter 7
a.why: The statement is the same as theorem 110 with two hypotheses in the other order, and it is the nontrivial direction of the textbook fact about the values of ℘.

b.states: Let L be a period pair and let z and w be complex numbers such that z, w, z − w and z + w all lie outside the lattice. Then ℘(z) − ℘(w) is nonzero. This is the statement of theorem 110 with the last two hypotheses in the other order.
b.known_as: ℘(z) = ℘(w) if and only if z ≡ ±w modulo the lattice (the direction that z ≢ ±w forces ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w))

check.known_as: ℘(z) = ℘(w) holds exactly when z ≡ ±w modulo L (the direction that z ≢ ±w forces ℘(z) ≠ ℘(w))
check.note: The statement repeats theorem 110 with the hypotheses z − w ∉ L and z + w ∉ L in the other order.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_open_nbhd_section_fiber_isPreirreducible
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, topology, homological algebra, combinatorics, geometry

a.states: Let f from X to S be a smooth morphism of schemes with a section e. For every point s of S there are an open U of X containing e(s), opens V₀ ⊆ V of S containing s, and a finite set I of functions on V that all vanish at s. These satisfy the following condition. For every t in V₀ at which all functions of I vanish, the part of the fibre f^{−1}(t) that lies in U is preirreducible, that is, irreducible or empty.
a.notation: ∀ s ∈ S, ∃ U ∋ e(s), ∃ V₀ ⊆ V ∋ s, ∃ I ⊆ Γ(V, 𝒪_S) finite with I(s) = 0, ∀ t ∈ V₀ ∩ V(I), U ∩ f^{−1}(t) is preirreducible
a.known_as: no published result known, a local statement on the irreducibility of fibres near a section of a smooth morphism, of the kind derived from Grothendieck's constructibility of geometric irreducibility of fibres in EGA IV
a.why: The finite set of vanishing functions cuts out a neighbourhood of s in a closed set through s, a shape that marks the statement as a step in a larger argument, and I know no source that states it.

b.states: Let f from X to S be a smooth morphism of schemes with a section e. For every point s of S there are an open U of X containing e(s), opens V₀ ⊆ V of S containing s, and a finite set I of sections of 𝒪_S over V that all vanish at s. For every t ∈ V₀ at which all members of I vanish, the part U ∩ f⁻¹(t) of the fibre over t is preirreducible. Adding members to I only shrinks the set of fibres that must be preirreducible, so the strongest form takes I empty.
b.known_as: Openness of the union X⁰ of the fibre components through a section of a smooth morphism, whose fibres are then irreducible (EGA IV_3 15.6.5, and SGA 3 Exp. VI_B 3.10 for group schemes), here in a local form

check.known_as: A weak local form of the openness of the union X⁰ of the connected components of the fibres that meet a section of a smooth morphism (EGA IV_3, §15.6, and SGA 3, Exp. VI_B, 3.10 for group schemes), whose fibres are irreducible because smooth fibres are normal
check.note: Adding members to the existential set I only shrinks the set of fibres that must be preirreducible, so the strongest form takes I empty, and that form follows with U = X⁰ and V₀ = V = S.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.TraitLift.exists_lift_adicCompletion
theorems.areas: ring theory

a.states: Let A be a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ with completion Â at its maximal ideal, and let V be a discrete valuation ring with a ring map from A. Then there are a complete discrete valuation ring V′, a ring map h from V to V′ that sends every uniformizer of V to a uniformizer of V′, and a ring map g from Â to V′. The restriction of g to A equals the composite A → V → V′.
a.notation: ∃ V′ complete DVR, ∃ h ∈ Hom(V, V′), ∃ g ∈ Hom(Â, V′), g ∘ (A → Â) = h ∘ (A → V) ∧ h(ϖ) is irreducible for every irreducible ϖ of V
a.known_as: no published result known, a lemma that extends a map from an excellent local ring to a discrete valuation ring over the completion of the local ring after an unramified enlargement of the valuation ring
a.why: The proof needs the formal fibres of A to be geometrically regular and the conclusion is tailored to a lifting argument, but I know no source that states it.

b.states: Let A be a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ, and let V be a discrete valuation ring with an arbitrary ring map from A to V. Then there are three things. The first is a discrete valuation ring V′ that is complete for its maximal ideal. The second is a ring map h from V to V′ that sends irreducible elements to irreducible elements. The third is a ring map g from the completion Â of A at its maximal ideal to V′ such that g composed with A → Â equals h composed with A → V.
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: No published result known, a lemma that extends a ring map from a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ to a discrete valuation ring over the completion of the local ring, after an enlargement of the valuation ring to a complete discrete valuation ring that keeps uniformizers
check.note: The map from A to V need not be local, and the content lies in that case, because for a local map the completion of V serves as V′.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.ferrand_glue_flat_artinian_fibreProduct
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, ring theory, homological algebra, combinatorics

a.states: Let P = R₁ ×_{R₀} R₂ be a fibre product of commutative rings along surjections R₁ → R₀ and R₂ → R₀, and let P be local and Artinian. Let Y₁ and Y₂ be flat schemes over Spec R₁ and Spec R₂ whose base changes to Spec R₀ are both identified with a scheme Y₀ over Spec R₀. Then there is a flat scheme Y over Spec P with maps from Y₁ and Y₂ that identify them with the base changes of Y to Spec R₁ and Spec R₂. Moreover, Y is the pushout of Y₁ and Y₂ along Y₀ in the category of schemes.
a.notation: Y = Y₁ ⊔_{Y₀} Y₂ is flat over Spec(R₁ ×_{R₀} R₂) and Y ×_{Spec P} Spec R_i ≅ Y_i for i = 1, 2
a.known_as: gluing of flat deformations over a fibre product of Artinian rings, Schlessinger's condition for deformations of schemes
a.reference: Michael Schlessinger, Functors of Artin rings, 1968
a.why: Schlessinger's gluing lemma needs only one of the two maps to be surjective. The Lean statement asks both to be surjective but also asserts the pushout property from Ferrand's pinching theory, so it is close to a special case without being exactly one.

b.states: Let P = R₁ ×_{R₀} R₂ be a pullback of commutative rings along surjections R₁ → R₀ and R₂ → R₀, with P local and Artinian. Let Y₁ be flat over Spec R₁ and Y₂ flat over Spec R₂, and suppose both base change to Spec R₀ give a scheme Y₀ through maps i₁ and i₂. Then there is a flat scheme Y over Spec P with maps j₁ and j₂ such that Y₁ and Y₂ are the base changes of Y to Spec R₁ and Spec R₂. This Y is also the pushout of i₁ and i₂ in the category of schemes.
b.known_as: Gluing of flat deformations over a fibre product of Artinian rings (Schlessinger 1968, Lemma 3.4 and conditions H1 and H2 for the deformation functor of a scheme), in the scheme form of Ferrand's pinching

check.known_as: Gluing of flat schemes over a fibre product of Artinian rings, the Schlessinger condition for the deformation functor of a scheme (Schlessinger 1968), together with Ferrand's pinching that makes the glued scheme a pushout
check.note: Surjectivity of R₁ → R₀ and R₂ → R₀ makes P → R₁ and P → R₂ surjective, so all four rings are local Artinian, while Schlessinger's gluing needs only one surjection, and the pushout claim comes from Ferrand's pinching along closed immersions.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.exists_field_cm_curves_unit_discriminant
theorems.areas: number fields, algebraic geometry, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, linear algebra, field theory

a.states: Let K be an imaginary quadratic field with a complex embedding σ. Then there is a number field M ⊆ ℂ containing σ(K) with the following property. For every lattice L ⊂ ℂ that is stable under multiplication by σ(𝒪_K), there is a Weierstrass curve W over 𝒪_M whose discriminant Δ(W) is a unit and whose j-invariant equals j(L). The equality of j-invariants is written as c₄(W)³ (g₂³ − 27g₃²) = 1728 g₂³ Δ(W).
a.notation: ∀ K imaginary quadratic, ∃ M ⊂ ℂ number field with σ(K) ⊆ M, ∀ L with σ(𝒪_K)L ⊆ L, ∃ W over 𝒪_M, Δ(W) ∈ 𝒪_M^× ∧ c₄(W)³ (g₂(L)³ − 27g₃(L)²) = 1728 g₂(L)³ Δ(W)
a.known_as: potential good reduction everywhere of elliptic curves with complex multiplication, strengthened to a single number field over which every curve with complex multiplication by 𝒪_K has a global Weierstrass model of unit discriminant
a.reference: Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties, 1968
a.why: The content beyond Serre and Tate, a global model of unit discriminant uniformly in L, follows from the finiteness of the j-invariants with complex multiplication by 𝒪_K and the capitulation of ideal classes in a Hilbert class field, and textbooks treat this as a known consequence rather than a named theorem.

b.states: Let K be a quadratic number field and σ a non-real embedding of K into ℂ, so K is imaginary quadratic. Then there is a number field M inside ℂ that contains σ(K) with the following property. For every period pair L whose lattice is stable under multiplication by σ(𝓞_K), there is a Weierstrass curve W over 𝓞_M with unit discriminant and c₄(W)³ (g₂³ − 27 g₃²) = 1728 g₂³ Δ(W). This identity says j(W) = j(L), so every elliptic curve with complex multiplication by 𝓞_K has a model over 𝓞_M with good reduction at every prime.
b.known_as: Potential good reduction everywhere of elliptic curves with complex multiplication (Deuring, Serre–Tate), strengthened to a global Weierstrass model with unit discriminant over one number field that serves all curves with CM by 𝓞_K

check.known_as: Potential good reduction everywhere of elliptic curves with complex multiplication (Deuring, Serre and Tate 1968), strengthened to one number field M over which every curve with complex multiplication by 𝓞_K has a Weierstrass model over 𝓞_M with unit discriminant
check.note: The polynomial identity says j(W) = j(L), because Δ(W) is a unit and g₂³ − 27g₃² ≠ 0, and a model with unit discriminant needs more than good reduction everywhere, namely a trivial class for the minimal discriminant, which an enlargement of M provides.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.SmoothDedekind.exists_isStandardSmoothOfRelativeDimension_of_isMaximal
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory, field theory, group theory

a.states: Let o be a Dedekind domain of characteristic zero that is finitely generated over ℤ, and let A be a flat finitely generated o-algebra. Suppose that every irreducible component of the generic fibre Frac(o) ⊗_o A has dimension at least d. Suppose also that r ≤ d for every algebraically closed field C and every ring map from A to the square-zero extension C ⊕ C^r whose C^r-part vanishes on o and spans C^r, which bounds by d the dimension of every relative tangent space of Spec A over o at a geometric point. Then every maximal ideal q of A has an element f outside q such that the localization A_f is standard smooth of relative dimension d over o.
a.notation: (∀ 𝔭 minimal in Frac(o) ⊗ A, dim (Frac(o) ⊗ A)/𝔭 ≥ d) ∧ (∀ x̄, dim T_{x̄}(Spec A / Spec o) ≤ d) ⇒ ∀ q maximal, ∃ f ∉ q, A_f is standard smooth of relative dimension d over o
a.known_as: no published result known, a smoothness criterion for flat finitely generated algebras over a Dedekind domain that combines the fibrewise criterion for smoothness with the Jacobian criterion on the fibres
a.why: Each ingredient is in EGA IV, but the specific hypotheses, a dimension bound on the generic fibre and a tangent space bound through square-zero extensions, are tailored to one application.

b.states: Let o be a Dedekind domain of characteristic zero and of finite type over ℤ, and let A be a flat o-algebra of finite type. Assume two things about A. Every irreducible component of the generic fibre Frac(o) ⊗_o A has Krull dimension at least d. At every geometric point of every fibre, the space of o-derivations into the residue field has dimension at most d, which the Lean text expresses through maps A → C ⊕ C^r with C^r of square zero whose second components span C^r. Then every maximal ideal q of A contains no element f outside it... more precisely, for every maximal ideal q there is an f ∉ q such that A_f is standard smooth of relative dimension d over o.
b.known_as: Smoothness criterion over a Dedekind base. A flat morphism of finite type is smooth of relative dimension d when every fibre has tangent spaces of dimension at most its local dimension d (fibrewise criterion EGA IV_4 17.5.1 together with the Jacobian criterion)

b_errors: B opens the conclusion with the garbled clause 'every maximal ideal q of A contains no element f outside it', which contradicts the Lean conclusion ∃ f ∉ q, Algebra.IsStandardSmoothOfRelativeDimension d o (Localization.Away f), although B corrects it in the same sentence.
check.known_as: No published result known, a smoothness criterion for flat finite-type algebras over a Dedekind domain assembled from the fibrewise criterion for smoothness (EGA IV_4 17.5.1), the tangent-space criterion on geometric fibres and the dimension theory of fibres of flat morphisms
check.note: The square-zero hypothesis says that dim_C Der_o(A, C) ≤ d at every geometric point, and flatness over the Dedekind base carries the lower bound d from the components of the generic fibre to the components of the closed fibres.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.exists_theta_division_point_ne_zero
theorems.areas: complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, topology, linear algebra

a.states: Let τ be a symmetric complex g × g matrix with positive definite imaginary part, let N ≥ 2, and let β₁, …, β_g be nonzero complex numbers. Let f be a nonzero entire function on ℂ^g with f(z + e_i) = f(z) and f(z + τe_j) = β_j exp(−2πi N z_j) f(z) for all i, j and z. Then there are integer vectors m and n with f((m + τn)/N) ≠ 0, so f does not vanish at every N-division point of the lattice ℤ^g + τℤ^g.
a.notation: f ≢ 0 entire, f(z + e_i) = f(z), f(z + τe_j) = β_j e^{−2πi N z_j} f(z), N ≥ 2 ⇒ ∃ m, n ∈ ℤ^g, f(N^{−1}(m + τn)) ≠ 0
a.known_as: no published result known, a statement that no nonzero theta function of level N ≥ 2 vanishes at all N-torsion points, which follows from the irreducibility of Mumford's theta group representation and the base point freeness of the N-th power of a principal polarization
a.why: The statement is a consequence of Mumford's theory of the theta group, but I know no textbook that states it in this form.

b.states: Let τ be a symmetric complex g×g matrix with positive definite imaginary part, let N ≥ 2, and let β be a vector of nonzero complex numbers. Let f be a nonzero entire function on ℂ^g with f(z + e_i) = f(z) and f(z + τe_j) = β_j exp(−2πi N z_j) f(z) for all i and j, so f is a theta function of level N. Then f(N⁻¹(m + τn)) ≠ 0 for some integer vectors m and n. In other words, f does not vanish at every N-division point of the period lattice.
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: No published result known, the statement that a nonzero theta function of level N ≥ 2 does not vanish at every N-division point, which follows from the irreducibility of the theta group representation and the base point freeness of the N-th power of a principal polarization
check.note: The arbitrary nonzero constants β_j allow every translate of the N-th power of the principal polarization, and the sections that vanish at all N-division points form a subspace stable under the theta group, which is zero by irreducibility and base point freeness.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.idealCharacterL_continuation_ne_zero_one
theorems.areas: number fields, complex analysis, inner product spaces, special functions, other analysis, topology, ring theory

a.states: Let K be a number field, m a nonzero ideal of 𝒪_K, and X a multiplicative function on ideals with X(0) = 0 that vanishes on ideals not coprime to m and has modulus 1 on nonzero ideals coprime to m. Let φ be a multiplicative function on K ⊗ ℝ that is invariant under positive real scalars and is smooth and of modulus 1 where the norm is nonzero, with X((β)) = φ(β) for every nonzero integer β ≡ 1 mod m, and assume X(J) ≠ 1 for some nonzero J coprime to m. Then for every function c on the primes with |c(P)| ≤ 1 and c(P) = X(P) for P not dividing m, there is a function L that is holomorphic on Re s > 0 with L(1) ≠ 0. For Re s > 1 this L equals the Euler product ∏_P (1 − c(P) N(P)^{−s})^{−1}, written as the exponential of a sum of logarithms.
a.notation: X a nontrivial unitary Grössencharacter mod m with infinity type φ, |c(P)| ≤ 1, c(P) = X(P) for P ∤ m ⇒ ∃ L holomorphic on {Re s > 0}, L(s) = ∏_P (1 − c(P) N(P)^{−s})^{−1} for Re s > 1 ∧ L(1) ≠ 0
a.known_as: Hecke's theorem on the analytic continuation of L-functions of nontrivial Grössencharacters and their nonvanishing at s = 1
a.reference: Erich Hecke, Eine neue Art von Zetafunktionen und ihre Beziehungen zur Verteilung der Primzahlen II, 1920
a.why: The hypotheses describe a unitary Grössencharacter whose infinity type is trivial on positive scalars, and the conclusion keeps only holomorphy on Re s > 0 and the nonzero value at 1 from Hecke's theorem. The encoding of the character is unusual, so the match needs care.

b.states: Let K be a number field, m a nonzero ideal of 𝓞_K and X a unitary Hecke character modulo m on ideals. Here X is completely multiplicative, has absolute value 1 on nonzero ideals prime to m and is zero on ideals not prime to m. On principal ideals (β) with β ≡ 1 mod m it equals φ(β) for a multiplicative, unimodular, smooth function φ on the mixed space ℝ^{r₁} × ℂ^{r₂} that is invariant under positive real scaling. If X(J) ≠ 1 for some nonzero J prime to m, then for any coefficients c(P) with |c(P)| ≤ 1 that equal X(P) at primes not dividing m, there is a function L that is holomorphic on Re s > 0, equals ∏_P (1 − c(P) N(P)^{−s})^{−1} (written as the exponential of a sum of −log terms) for Re s > 1, and satisfies L(1) ≠ 0.
b.known_as: Analytic continuation of the L-function of a nontrivial Größencharakter (Hecke) together with its non-vanishing at s = 1

check.known_as: Hecke's theorem on the analytic continuation of L-functions of nontrivial Grössencharacters, together with their nonvanishing at s = 1
check.note: Invariance of φ under positive real scalars rules out characters of the form N(I)^{it}, whose L-functions have a pole on Re s = 1, and the Euler factors at the primes dividing m may use any c(P) of modulus at most 1.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.AbMonoIso.isIso_of_isClosedImmersion
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, combinatorics

a.states: Let S be a locally noetherian scheme and let p from X to S be smooth of relative dimension g′ with geometrically connected fibres. Let f from Y to X be a closed immersion such that the composite Y → S is surjective, flat and smooth of relative dimension g with g′ ≤ g. Then f is an isomorphism.
a.notation: f closed immersion, p smooth of relative dimension g′ with geometrically connected fibres, p ∘ f surjective, flat and smooth of relative dimension g ≥ g′ ⇒ f is an isomorphism
a.known_as: no published result known, a fibrewise criterion showing that a closed subscheme that meets every fibre and is smooth over S of no smaller relative dimension fills a smooth scheme with connected fibres
a.vacuity: No hypothesis is impossible, though the flatness of the composite is redundant because its smoothness implies it.
a.why: The proof combines the fact that a smooth closed subscheme of the same dimension is open and closed in each fibre with the fibrewise criterion for isomorphisms in EGA IV, and this combination is shaped for one use.

b.states: Let S be a locally Noetherian scheme, let p from X to S be smooth of relative dimension g′ with geometrically connected fibres, and let f from Y to X be a closed immersion. Suppose f followed by p is surjective, flat and smooth of relative dimension g, with g′ ≤ g. Then f is an isomorphism. The flatness hypothesis already follows from smoothness.
b.known_as: no published result known

check.known_as: No published result known, a criterion that a closed subscheme which is surjective and smooth over S of relative dimension at least that of a smooth S-scheme with geometrically connected fibres is the whole scheme
check.note: The flatness hypothesis follows from smoothness of the composite, and dimension forces g = g′, so f is an étale closed immersion whose image is open and closed in each connected fibre.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.formalFibre_isReduced_of_field
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let A be a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ, and let L be a field with a ring map from A. Then the tensor product over A of the completion of A at its maximal ideal with L is a reduced ring.
a.notation: Â ⊗_A L is reduced for every field L that is an A-algebra
a.known_as: geometric reducedness of the formal fibres of an excellent local ring, here for local rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which Grothendieck proved to be excellent
a.reference: Alexander Grothendieck, Éléments de géométrie algébrique IV, Seconde partie, 1965
a.why: Rings essentially of finite type over ℤ are excellent, so their formal fibres are geometrically regular and hence geometrically reduced, and the Lean statement keeps only reducedness after base change to a field.

b.states: Let A be a local ring essentially of finite type over ℤ and L any field with a ring map from A to L. Then Â ⊗_A L is reduced, where Â is the completion of A at its maximal ideal. This is the same as saying that all formal fibres of A are geometrically reduced.
b.known_as: Geometric reducedness of the formal fibres of an excellent local ring, here for local rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent by Grothendieck (EGA IV_2 7.8.3)

check.known_as: Geometric reducedness of the formal fibres of an excellent local ring, for local rings essentially of finite type over ℤ, which are excellent (EGA IV_2 7.8.3)
check.note: The field L is arbitrary, so the statement covers every field extension of every residue field of A and says that all formal fibres of A are geometrically reduced.

theorems.name: Formalism.MainNotions.CrystallineLiftingInputs.rem_2
theorems.areas: ring theory

a.states: Take a commutative ring R, a natural number l ≥ 1, elements π₀, q, u, ε of R, and natural numbers y, X, c with y ≥ 1 and c + ⌊(X − 1)/l⌋ ≤ (l − 1)y. Then the element (π₀ q^{l−1} (u q^l + l ε)^{l−1})^y lies in the ideal of R generated by l^c and π₀ q^X. Here X − 1 is truncated subtraction in ℕ, the quotient is floor division, and l also stands for its image in R.
a.notation: R comm. ring, l ≥ 1, π₀, q, u, ε ∈ R, y ≥ 1, c + ⌊(X ∸ 1)/l⌋ ≤ (l − 1)y ⟹ (π₀ q^{l−1} (u q^l + lε)^{l−1})^y ∈ (l^c, π₀ q^X)
a.known_as: no published result known, an elementary ideal-membership estimate proved by a binomial expansion
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example with l = 2, y = 1, c = 1 and X = 1, and when l = 1 they force c = 0, so l^c = 1 and the conclusion holds trivially.
a.why: In the binomial expansion of (u q^l + lε)^{(l−1)y}, the term with k factors u q^l lies in (l^c) when (l − 1)y − k ≥ c, and otherwise k > ⌊(X − 1)/l⌋ gives at least X factors of q next to π₀, so the statement is a routine computation shaped for one proof.

b.states: Let R be a commutative ring, let l, y, X and c be natural numbers with 1 ≤ l and 1 ≤ y, and let π₀, q, u and ε be elements of R. Suppose c + (X − 1)/l ≤ (l − 1)·y, where the subtraction and the division are truncated operations on natural numbers. Then the element (π₀·q^(l−1)·(u·q^l + l·ε)^(l−1))^y lies in the ideal of R generated by l^c and π₀·q^X.
b.known_as: no published result known
b.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses hold for instance with l = 2, y = 1, X = 1 and c = 1, and the ideal is the whole ring only when c = 0.

check.known_as: no published result known, an elementary ideal-membership estimate proved by a binomial expansion
check.vacuity: None found, since the hypotheses hold for instance with l = 2, y = 1, c = 1 and X = 1, although the conclusion is immediate when c = 0, which l = 1 forces, or when l is a unit in R.
check.note: The quotient (X − 1)/l is floor division of natural numbers, and the membership is immediate when X ≤ (l − 1)y because the element has the factor π₀q^{(l−1)y}, so the hypothesis does real work only for larger X, where the binomial expansion of (u q^l + lε)^{(l−1)y} is needed.

theorems.name: Formalism.MainNotions.CrystallineLiftingInputs.rem_M
theorems.areas: ring theory

a.states: Take a commutative ring R, a natural number l ≥ 1, an element π₀ of R, and natural numbers y, M, η, c with c + η + M ≤ l y. Then the element (π₀ (π₀ + l)^{l−1})^y lies in the ideal of R generated by l^c and π₀^M (π₀ + l)^η. Here l also stands for its image in R.
a.notation: R comm. ring, l ≥ 1, π₀ ∈ R, c + η + M ≤ l y ⟹ (π₀ (π₀ + l)^{l−1})^y ∈ (l^c, π₀^M (π₀ + l)^η)
a.known_as: no published result known, an elementary ideal-membership estimate proved by a binomial expansion
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example with l = 3, y = 1, c = 1, M = 2 and η = 0, and when l = 1 the generator l^c equals 1, so the conclusion holds trivially.
a.why: With t = π₀ + l the element is π₀^y t^{(l−1)y}, which has total degree l y in π₀ and t, and expanding the surplus factor binomially through l = t − π₀ puts every term into (l^c) or into (π₀^M t^η) because c + η + M ≤ l y, so the statement is a routine computation shaped for one proof.

b.states: Let R be a commutative ring, let l, y, M, η and c be natural numbers with 1 ≤ l and c + η + M ≤ l·y, and let π₀ be an element of R. Then the element (π₀·(π₀ + l)^(l−1))^y lies in the ideal of R generated by l^c and π₀^M·(π₀ + l)^η.
b.known_as: no published result known
b.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses hold for instance with l = 2, y = 1, c = 1, η = 0 and M = 1, and the ideal is the whole ring only when c = 0.

check.known_as: no published result known, an elementary ideal-membership estimate proved by a binomial expansion in π₀ and π₀ + l
check.vacuity: None found, since the hypotheses hold for instance with l = 2, y = 1, c = 1, M = 1 and η = 0, although the conclusion is immediate when l = 1 or c = 0, because then l^c = 1.
check.note: With t = π₀ + l the element is π₀^y t^{(l−1)y}, whose total degree l·y in π₀ and t is at least c + M + η by the hypothesis, and that degree count is all the statement uses.

theorems.name: Formalism.MainNotions.RamifiedCoefficientChains.S9.DetD.length_coker_le
theorems.areas: linear algebra, ring theory

a.states: Let O be a discrete valuation ring, QQ an r × r matrix over O, l a nonzero element of O, and V a natural number such that det QQ divides l^V. Then the length of the O-module O^r / QQ·O^r, which is the cokernel of the linear map given by QQ, is at most V times the length of O/(l), with lengths taken in ℕ ∪ {∞}. None of the section variables in scope, such as the period data and the module W, occurs in the statement, and the theorem binds its own ring O.
a.notation: O DVR, QQ ∈ M_r(O), l ≠ 0, det QQ | l^V ⟹ length_O(O^r / QQ O^r) ≤ V · length_O(O/lO)
a.known_as: the formula that the length of the cokernel of an injective endomorphism of O^r over a discrete valuation ring equals the valuation of its determinant
a.reference: William Fulton, Intersection Theory, 1984, Appendix A.2
a.why: Over a discrete valuation ring the Smith normal form gives length(coker QQ) = v(det QQ), and det QQ | l^V gives v(det QQ) ≤ V·v(l) = V·length(O/(l)), so the Lean bound follows at once from the standard formula and is shaped around a divisibility hypothesis that a larger proof supplies.

b.states: Let O be a discrete valuation ring, let r be a natural number, let QQ be an r×r matrix over O, let l be a nonzero element of O and let V be a natural number such that det QQ divides l^V. Then the length of the O-module O^r modulo the image of QQ is at most V times the length of O/(l), computed in the extended natural numbers.
b.known_as: over a discrete valuation ring the length of the cokernel of a square matrix with nonzero determinant equals the valuation of the determinant (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Lemma A.2.6)
b.vacuity: None found, and the project variable W of type LocWach in the variable lines does not occur in the statement, so it does not enter it.

check.known_as: the formula that over a discrete valuation ring the length of the cokernel of a square matrix with nonzero determinant equals the valuation of the determinant
check.note: The divisibility det QQ ∣ l^V with l ≠ 0 forces det QQ ≠ 0, so the cokernel has finite length equal to the valuation of det QQ, and the bound follows from v(det QQ) ≤ V·v(l), while the section variable W and the period data do not enter the statement.

theorems.name: GroundTheory.ProfCoh.eq_zero_of_forall_sylow_map_eq_zero
theorems.areas: representation theory, category theory, group theory, homological algebra

a.states: Let k be a commutative ring, G a finite group, A a k-linear representation of G, and n ≥ 1. Suppose a class x in the group cohomology H^n(G, A) restricts to zero on some Sylow p-subgroup P of G for every prime p dividing |G|. Then x = 0. The restriction here is the map H^n(G, A) → H^n(P, A) induced by the inclusion of P into G and the identity of A.
a.notation: n ≥ 1, x ∈ H^n(G, A), ∀ p | |G| ∃ P ∈ Syl_p(G) with res^G_P x = 0 ⟹ x = 0
a.known_as: injectivity of restriction to a Sylow p-subgroup on the p-primary part of H^n(G, A) for n ≥ 1, in its corollary form that a class vanishing on all Sylow subgroups is zero
a.reference: Kenneth S. Brown, Cohomology of Groups, 1982, Chapter III, Section 10
a.vacuity: None found, and for the trivial group the hypothesis is empty but the conclusion still holds because H^n vanishes there for n ≥ 1.
a.why: The textbook argument uses cor∘res = [G : P] to show that restriction to a Sylow p-subgroup is injective on the p-primary part of the |G|-torsion group H^n(G, A) for n ≥ 1, and the Lean statement is that corollary, because the cohomology of a k-linear representation has the same underlying abelian group as the cohomology of the underlying G-module.

b.states: Let k be a commutative ring, let G be a finite group, let A be a k-linear representation of G, let n ≥ 1 and let x be a class in H^n(G, A). Suppose that for every prime p dividing the order of G there is a Sylow p-subgroup P such that the restriction of x to P is zero. Then x = 0.
b.known_as: injectivity of restriction to the Sylow subgroups in positive-degree cohomology of finite groups, so a class whose restrictions to all Sylow subgroups vanish is zero (Brown, Cohomology of Groups III.10.4, Cassels and Fröhlich IV.6)

check.known_as: injectivity of restriction to a Sylow p-subgroup on the p-primary part of positive-degree cohomology of a finite group, in the form that a class whose restriction to one Sylow p-subgroup vanishes for every prime p is zero
check.note: The statement concerns ordinary cohomology in degree n ≥ 1 of a representation over any commutative ring k, and the restriction is Mathlib's groupCohomology.map along the inclusion of P with the identity on A.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.T.holomorphic_disc_ratio_growth
theorems.areas: complex analysis, other analysis, topology, ring theory

a.states: Let Ω be a field of characteristic zero and A a finitely generated ℚ-subalgebra of Ω that is smooth over ℚ and such that every element of Ω is a fraction a/b with a, b ∈ A and b ≠ 0, so Ω is the fraction field of A. Let g, h, b ∈ A with h ≠ 0, b ≠ 0 and g/h ∉ A. Then there are a map ψ from ℂ to the set of ring homomorphisms A → ℂ and a real constant C such that z ↦ ψ(z)(a) is holomorphic on the open unit disc for every a ∈ A. Moreover, for every z ≠ 0 in that disc, ψ(z)(b) ≠ 0, ψ(z)(h) ≠ 0 and |ψ(z)(h)| ≤ C|z||ψ(z)(g)|.
a.notation: A ⊆ Ω = Frac A f.g. smooth over ℚ, h, b ≠ 0, g/h ∉ A ⟹ ∃ holomorphic ψ: 𝔻 → (Spec A)(ℂ), ∃ C, ∀ z ∈ 𝔻∖{0}, b(ψ(z)) ≠ 0, h(ψ(z)) ≠ 0, |h(ψ(z))| ≤ C|z||g(ψ(z))|
a.known_as: no published result known, a holomorphic-disc witness that a rational function g/h which is not regular on a smooth affine ℚ-variety has a pole, in the spirit of the Riemann extension theorem
a.vacuity: The hypotheses can be met, for example with A = ℚ[t] in Ω = ℚ(t), g = b = 1 and h = t, and the conclusion forces ψ to be nonconstant, because a constant ψ with h(ψ) ≠ 0 would break the bound as z tends to 0.
a.why: The statement follows from two facts, that a normal Noetherian domain is the intersection of its localizations at height-one primes and that a disc crossing the polar divisor of g/h transversally at a general smooth point sees a pole of order at least one, but I know no source that states this disc form, and Theorem 137 proves the same conclusion for normal rings.

b.states: Let Ω be a field that is a ℚ-algebra, and let A be a ℚ-subalgebra of Ω that is finitely generated and smooth over ℚ and has Ω as its field of fractions. Let g, h and b be elements of A with h ≠ 0, b ≠ 0 and g/h not in A. Then there exist a family ψ of ring homomorphisms from A to ℂ, indexed by z in ℂ, and a real number C such that z ↦ ψ z a is holomorphic on the open unit disc for every a in A. Moreover, for every z ≠ 0 in that disc, ψ z b ≠ 0, ψ z h ≠ 0 and |ψ z h| ≤ C·|z|·|ψ z g|, so the disc runs into a pole of g/h at its centre.
b.known_as: no published result known
b.vacuity: None found, because the hypotheses hold for instance with Ω = ℚ(t), A = ℚ[t], g = 1, h = t and b = 1.

check.known_as: no published result known, a holomorphic disc that runs into the polar divisor of a rational function g/h which is not regular on a smooth affine ℚ-variety
check.vacuity: None found, since the hypotheses hold for instance with Ω = ℚ(t), A = ℚ[t], g = b = 1 and h = t.
check.note: Continuity of ψ at 0 and the bound force ψ(0)(h) = 0, so the disc is centred on the zero set of h where g/h has its pole, and theorem 137 proves the same conclusion for every Noetherian integrally closed finitely generated ℚ-domain, which covers this smooth case.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.WeberSplit.invariant_isAlgebraic
theorems.areas: number fields, complex analysis, special functions, other analysis, linear algebra, ring theory, field theory

a.states: Let K be a subfield of ℂ of degree 2 over ℚ, and let L be a period pair, which is a basis ω₁, ω₂ of a lattice in ℂ, whose lattice is exactly the image of the ring of integers 𝓞_K. Then g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) is algebraic over ℚ, where g₂ and g₃ are the Weierstrass invariants of L. This quotient equals j/1728, so the statement says that the j-invariant of the lattice 𝓞_K is algebraic. The lattice hypothesis forces K to be imaginary quadratic.
a.notation: K ⊆ ℂ, [K : ℚ] = 2, Λ_L = 𝓞_K ⟹ g₂(L)³/(g₂(L)³ − 27g₃(L)²) = j(𝓞_K)/1728 ∈ ℚ̄
a.known_as: algebraicity of singular moduli, the theorem of complex multiplication that the j-invariant of a lattice with complex multiplication by an order of an imaginary quadratic field is an algebraic integer
a.reference: David A. Cox, Primes of the Form x² + ny², 1989, Theorem 11.1
a.vacuity: The lattice hypothesis cannot hold for a real quadratic K, because 𝓞_K then lies in ℝ and is not a lattice, but it holds for a suitable period pair for every imaginary quadratic K, so the statement is not empty.
a.why: The Lean statement is the algebraicity of j(𝓞_K)/1728 for the maximal order alone, which is the narrowest instance of the classical theorem, and the quotient g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²) is exactly j/1728.

b.states: Let K be a subfield of ℂ that is a number field of degree 2 over ℚ, and let L be a period pair whose lattice is exactly the image in ℂ of the ring of integers of K. Then the number g₂³/(g₂³ − 27·g₃²), formed from the invariants of L, is algebraic over ℚ. This number is j(L)/1728.
b.known_as: algebraicity of the j-invariant of a lattice with complex multiplication, the first part of the main theorem of complex multiplication, here for the lattice 𝓞_K of an imaginary quadratic field
b.vacuity: The hypothesis hL cannot be met when K is real quadratic, because then 𝓞_K lies in ℝ and is no lattice, so the statement has content only for imaginary quadratic K.

check.known_as: algebraicity of singular moduli, the part of the theory of complex multiplication that says j(𝓞_K) is an algebraic integer for an imaginary quadratic field K
check.vacuity: None found, because hL can be met for every imaginary quadratic field K and fails only for real quadratic K, where 𝓞_K lies in ℝ and is no lattice.
check.note: The quotient equals j(𝓞_K)/1728 and is a genuine quotient because g₂³ − 27g₃² never vanishes for a lattice, and the statement covers only the lattice 𝓞_K itself, not other orders or ideal classes.

theorems.name: GlobalTheory.AbMonoIsoAny.isIso_of_isClosedImmersion
theorems.areas: algebraic geometry, category theory, combinatorics

a.states: Let S, X, Y be schemes, let p: X → S be a morphism with geometrically connected fibres, and let f: Y → X be a closed immersion such that the composite p∘f: Y → S is surjective. Suppose that p is smooth of relative dimension g′ and that p∘f is smooth of relative dimension g with g′ ≤ g. Then f is an isomorphism.
a.notation: f: Y ↪ X closed, p: X → S smooth of rel. dim g′ with geometrically connected fibres, p∘f surjective and smooth of rel. dim g ≥ g′ ⟹ f is an isomorphism
a.known_as: no published result known in this form, a fibrewise dimension criterion for a closed immersion of smooth S-schemes to be an isomorphism, of the kind used to show that a monomorphism of abelian schemes of equal dimension is an isomorphism
